title: The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering

paper.title: The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering
paper.abstract: Abstract Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the dominant paradigm for grounding large language models in external corpora, but its similarity-driven, chunked pipeline has structural blind spots: it cannot anticipate which passages a question requires and discards document-level context that resolves cross-passage references. We introduce evidence-based generation (EBG), requiring models to return an answer with line-level citations, and a joint Ans+Evid metric that scores correctness and grounding simultaneously. We reformulate two corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document QA benchmarks - MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP , a multi-paper adaptation of QASPER with realistic short paper cues, and pair them with a controlled synthetic two-hop haystack and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K–1M characters. Across ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs, EBG isolates two RAG limitations that long-context models avoid: similarity retrieval surfaces any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi-fact queries, and chunking destroys document meta-information needed to resolve identity-bearing queries. EBG also exposes grounding failures invisible to answer-only evaluation, including incomplete citations in two-needle settings and a widening gap between Ans and Ans+Evid when context contradicts parametric knowledge. Data and code are available at https://github.com/debobanerjee/LC-EBG .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) can rapidly process large text volumes to identify information relevant to a query. This capability suits applications such as legal discovery, medical analysis, financial due diligence, literature review, etc., which require synthesis from large document collections. The predominant paradigm for grounding LLM outputs in external knowledge is retrieval-augmented generation ( Lewis et al., 2020 , RAG;) , which retrieves passages via embedding similarity and conditions the generator on those passages alone. While effective for single-fact lookups , this design has several structural limitations. First, each retrieved chunk is stripped of its surrounding context: the model cannot see where a paragraph falls within a document or how it relates to neighboring sections. Second, document-level metadata (authorship, date, section hierarchy) is typically lost during chunking. Third, and most critically, similarity-based retrieval cannot anticipate which combination of passages will be needed for questions requiring integration across multiple locations. This is particularly acute for multi-hop questions , where the answer depends on chaining facts that may appear in distant, semantically dissimilar passages ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Our goal in this paper is not to advocate replacing RAG with long-context (LC) models outright, but to make these structural limitations measurable. RAG systems are typically evaluated on answer correctness alone, which conflates two very different failure modes: the retriever fails to surface the right passages, or the reader fails to use them. To separate the two, we propose evidence-based generation (EBG) , a paradigm where the model must produce both an answer and explicit references to the input lines that support it. EBG inherits RAG’s built-in verifiability ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) , but extends it to long-context settings where the model is given the full document neighborhood and must select its own evidence. The joint Ans+Evid metric pinpoints where a pipeline breaks: in retrieval, in grounding, or in reading. Recent work shows LC models can match or exceed RAG accuracy given sufficient context ( Li et al., 2024 ; Laitenberger et al., 2025 ) , but without provenance these comparisons are inconclusive; EBG closes that gap. We make the following contributions: • EBG framework. We define the evidence-based generation task and a joint Ans+Evid metric, and evaluate ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs under matched LC and RAG conditions across 10K–1M character contexts. • Evidence-grounded benchmarks. We reformulate two corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document QA benchmarks—a re-instrumented MultiHop-RAG with line-level evidence labels, and QASPER-MP , a multi-paper QASPER adaptation with realistic paper cues, and pair them with a controlled two-hop synthetic haystack and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa . The first two stress retrieval; the last two stress long-context reading. • Characterizing RAG’s limitations. Using EBG, we isolate two failure modes of similarity-based RAG that LC sidesteps: (i) retrieval recovers any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi-fact queries, and (ii) chunking discards document meta-information that identity-bearing queries depend on. On MultiHop-RAG , the retrieval ceiling at realistic top-k budgets, not the reader, is the binding constraint. • Diagnostic analysis of LC grounding. Beyond the RAG comparison, EBG reveals that citation acts as a reasoning scaffold, that models cite incomplete evidence in two-needle settings, and that grounding degrades sharply when in-context evidence contradicts parametric knowledge.

sections.heading: 2.1 Long-Context Language Models
sections.text: Advances in transformer architectures have expanded context windows from thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens through improved positional encoding such as ALiBi ( Press et al., 2022 ) , RoPE extensions ( Su et al., 2024 ) , and memory-augmented attention ( Wu et al., 2022 ) . Training data matters equally, as pretraining corpora rarely contain long-range dependencies; Zhuang et al. (2025) construct data with long-distance references encouraging use of distant context. Yet larger windows do not automatically yield better reasoning. Du et al. (2025) show accuracy degrades with context length even under perfect retrieval, suggesting a processing bottleneck. Similarly, Liu et al. (2024) show performance drops when information appears mid-input rather than at boundaries.

sections.heading: 2.2 Evaluating Long-Context Reasoning
sections.text: Early long-context evaluations relied on needle-in-a-haystack tests ( Kamradt, 2024 ) , which mainly measure retrieval of planted information rather than reasoning. Subsequent work argues that such evaluations set the bar too low, since strong performance often reflects shallow heuristics rather than genuine understanding ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Schuster et al., 2025 ; Modarressi et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Yen et al., 2025 ) . Recent benchmarks shift toward more demanding evaluations: ∞ \infty Bench ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) studies degradation beyond 100K characters, HELMET ( Yen et al., 2025 ) shows that benchmark choice substantially alters rankings, and NoLiMa ( Modarressi et al., 2025 ) removes lexical shortcuts by requiring semantic matching between queries and evidence. However, these benchmarks still score models on final answers alone, leaving open whether correct answers stem from actual use of relevant context or from priors, surface cues, or chance. Unlike these answer-only benchmarks, our work focuses on grounding by requiring models to return both answers and supporting input lines, distinguishing genuine reasoning from lucky guessing and enabling a more faithful assessment of whether models use long contexts effectively and reliably.

sections.heading: 2.3 Retrieval-Augmented Generation
sections.text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) remains the dominant approach for grounding LLMs in external knowledge. Built on dense retrieval ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ) and multi-passage readers such as Fusion-in-Decoder ( Izacard and Grave, 2021 ) , RAG provides provenance by construction since retrieved passages serve as evidence. Recent work revisits RAG alongside long-context models, highlighting a trade-off between the two paradigms ( Li et al., 2024 ; Laitenberger et al., 2025 ) : long-context prompting generally improves accuracy but at substantially higher cost, motivating hybrid systems that route queries by difficulty ( Li et al., 2024 ) . Controlled comparisons also show well-tuned single-stage RAG can match elaborate multi-stage pipelines once token budgets are equalized ( Laitenberger et al., 2025 ) , while adaptive retrieval and self-reflection improve factuality and citation quality ( Asai et al., 2024 ) . Existing work primarily evaluates these approaches on accuracy or efficiency. We instead focus on grounding, distinguishing whether evidence was available from whether the model actually used it.

sections.heading: 3 Evidence-based Generation (EBG)
sections.text: We formalize evidence-based generation (EBG) as a grounded question-answering paradigm that extends standard answer-only evaluation by requiring models to generate both answers and explicit citations to the supporting input evidence.

sections.heading: 3.1 Answer-only vs Evidence-based Generation
sections.text: Existing long-context evaluations, including NoLiMa ( Modarressi et al., 2025 ) , use answer-only evaluation, omitting the grounding needed to validate model reasoning. EBG extends this formulation by requiring models to generate both explicit evidence references to supporting input lines and the final answer , yielding a stricter evaluation setting in which correctness depends on both accurate reasoning and faithful grounding. To illustrate the distinction, consider a haystack containing the sentence “Then Stuart mentioned that he has been vegan for years.” at line 1,284 and the question “Which character cannot eat Brandade?” - a two-hop query requiring the inference that Brandade contains fish and is therefore incompatible with veganism . The answer-only and EBG settings differ in both the system instruction and the required output format. Answer-only Prompt (User) You will answer a question based on the following book snippet: {haystack} Use the information provided in the book snippet to answer the question. Your answer should be short and based on either explicitly stated facts or strong, logical inferences. Question: Which character cannot eat Brandade? Return only the final answer with no additional explanation or reasoning. Model Response Stuart Under answer-only evaluation, the response ‘‘Stuart’’ is simply marked correct. But under EBG, the same response is evaluated using three complementary metrics: answer accuracy ( Ans ), evidence accuracy ( Evid ), and their conjunction ( Ans+Evid ). While Ans preserves standard answer correctness, Ans+Evid additionally requires the model to cite the supporting evidence at line 1,284. Together, these metrics separate answer correctness from evidence-grounded correctness. EBG Prompt (System + User) [system] Your job is to answer the question entirely from the context and provide a reference. Your answer should cite all lines the answer is based on. [user] <context>{haystack}</context> Answer the question based on information only from the context. If the question is not answerable from the context, answer NA. Your response should comprise only the answer and all lines the answer is based on in json format. For example: { ‘‘lines’’: [25, 412],‘‘answer’’: ‘‘John’’ } Question: Which character cannot eat Brandade? Model Response { ‘‘lines’’: [1284], ‘‘answer’’: ‘‘Stuart’’ } This decomposition exposes silent failures hidden by answer-only evaluation: a model may arrive at the correct answer while citing irrelevant lines, or retrieve the correct evidence while producing the wrong answer. The joint Ans+Evid metric therefore serves as the strictest measure of evidence-based reasoning, requiring both accurate reasoning and faithful grounding. We also evaluate vanilla Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, following Modarressi et al. (2025) , and a CoT-based EBG prompting variant. The prompt templates are in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 3.2 RAG under EBG
sections.text: In this work, we evaluate RAG systems within the EBG framework by requiring models to not only answer using retrieved chunks, but also to explicitly cite the supporting evidence. This yields two RAG variants: • Answer-only RAG: Standard formulation requiring answer correctness only. • Answer + Evidence RAG: EBG formulation requiring correct answer and correct citation. This unified view allows us to decompose end-to-end performance into two factors: • Evidence availability: whether the retriever surfaces the relevant needle(s) (Hit@k), • Evidence utilization: whether the model correctly uses and cites the retrieved evidence (long-context accuracy). Overall, our formulation shows that RAG and EBG are not competing paradigms but complementary components : retrieval determines what evidence is available , while EBG determines whether that evidence is correctly used and cited .

sections.heading: 4 Benchmarks
sections.text: To systematically evaluate EBG and RAG under EBG, we construct four complementary benchmarks: a fully synthetic benchmark, an evidence-augmented version of NoLiMa, MultiHop-RAG, and QASPER-MP (an adapted version of QASPER). Together, they evaluate EBG under both controlled synthetic settings and realistic long-context scenarios.

sections.heading: 4.1 Synthetic Dataset
sections.text: The synthetic benchmark provides precise control over haystack content and evidence placement. It consists of a distractor fact pool, a curated needle set, and a haystack generation procedure. This controlled construction allows us to vary context length independently of task difficulty while retaining exact ground-truth evidence locations.

sections.heading: Distractor fact pool.
sections.text: We construct a fixed pool of 66,834 unique single-sentence facts using iterative LLM prompting followed by deduplication, ensuring that distractors are not confusable with inserted needles. The large pool also limits repeated distractors across independently generated trials and provides sufficient diversity for constructing long haystacks.

sections.heading: Needle set.
sections.text: We manually curate 10 two-hop needles , each containing: i) two atomic supporting facts, ii) a compositional question requiring both facts, and iii) accepted answer surface forms. The needles span relations such as company–product associations, founder–specialty links, and birthplace lookups. By requiring composition across two independently placed facts, the benchmark tests both evidence retrieval and integration rather than simple single-fact recall.

sections.heading: Haystack assembly.
sections.text: For a target length L L , distractor facts are shuffled and accumulated until reaching L L characters, after which the two needle facts are inserted at independently sampled positions and recorded as gold evidence. Haystacks are formatted as line-numbered i: fact entries and evaluated under the EBG prompt template (§ A ). Each trial uses a newly generated haystack and a uniformly sampled needle. Consequently, performance differences cannot be attributed to a fixed ordering of distractors or evidence positions. Appendix B.1 provides a representative example.

sections.heading: Sanity check.
sections.text: At L = 10 ​ K L{=}10\text{K} ( ≈ 2 ​ K {\approx}2\text{K} tokens), all evaluated frontier models achieve at least 0.98 0.98 joint Ans+Evid accuracy over N = 100 N{=}100 trials, confirming that the inserted needles are unambiguous and readily solvable when context length is modest. Any degradation at larger L L therefore reflects failures in long-context evidence retrieval or integration rather than intrinsic task ambiguity. This makes the synthetic benchmark a controlled probe of how model reliability changes as relevant evidence becomes increasingly sparse within the surrounding context.

sections.heading: 4.2 NoLiMa-based Dataset
sections.text: We adapt the NoLiMa haystack construction procedure to create long-context inputs ranging from L = 10 ​ K L{=}10\text{K} to 1 ​ M 1\text{M} characters and require models to both answer questions and cite supporting needles as evidence. This converts NoLiMa from an answer-only benchmark into an evidence-grounded evaluation that tests whether models truly use the provided context.

sections.heading: Needle set.
sections.text: We use the original single-needle (SN) setting from NoLiMa ( Modarressi et al., 2025 ) , specifically the 0402 and 0405 needle groups with both default and inverse variants under the commonsense category. Each needle contains a character name and a single factual attribute, and supports both one-hop and two-hop questions. We further introduce a two-needle ( TN ) setting, in which the explicit secondary needle is consistent with world knowledge, and a contradictory two-needle ( CTN ) variant, in which it conflicts with world knowledge. Appendix C.1 provides additional details and templates for SN , TN , and CTN settings.

sections.heading: Haystack assembly.
sections.text: We adopt the random book generation procedure from NoLiMa ( Modarressi et al., 2025 ) to construct haystacks ranging from 10K to 1M characters (10K–50K in 10K increments and 100K–1M in 100K increments), generating three random books B 1 c , B 2 c , B 3 c {B^{c}_{1},B^{c}_{2},B^{c}_{3}} for each context length c c . Because tokenization is model-dependent, we vary input length in characters rather than tokens. Each haystack is split into line-indexed entries using the ‘\n’ delimiter. In the single-needle setting, the needle is inserted at one of four normalized depths: 0, 0.33, 0.67, or 1.0. In the two-needle setting, the primary needle is fixed at depth 0.5, while the secondary needle is inserted at one of the same four depths.

sections.heading: 4.3 Multi-document QA Datasets
sections.text: To stress the retrieval pipeline on the dimensions it is meant to handle, we reformulate two existing corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document question answering (QA) benchmarks. Both are designed to make RAG’s retrieval-vs.-reading split observable: gold evidence is labeled at the line (sentence or paragraph) level, so the same scoring code works for LC and any retriever-ordered context.

sections.heading: MultiHop-RAG ( Tang and Yang, 2024 ) .
sections.text: The official release contains 609 news articles (4.6M characters, 1.2M tokens with the cl100k_base tokenizer) and 2,556 queries in four templated types: inference , comparison , temporal , and null_query (unanswerable). Each non-null query carries an evidence_list of 2–4 gold facts , each consisting of a source article title and an exact textual span. Removing the 301 null_query items leaves 2,255 usable queries ; for the pilot reported in this paper, we uniformly sample 50 queries (seed 0), naturally stratified across the three answerable types ( n inf = 13 n_{\text{inf}}{=}13 , n comp = 21 n_{\text{comp}}{=}21 , n temp = 16 n_{\text{temp}}{=}16 ). For the LC condition, we construct an oracle-containing per-query mini-haystack comprising every gold-evidence article plus 20 distractor articles sampled from the remainder of the corpus. The articles are concatenated in random order and split into sentence-per-line entries, producing contexts of approximately 241K characters on average. For the RAG condition, we perform open-corpus retrieval over the full 609-article corpus: we divide the corpus into 256-token sliding windows (6,296 chunks), embed the chunks with text-embedding-3-large , and rank them by cosine similarity to produce top- K K contexts for K ∈ { 4 , 10 , 25 , 50 , 100 , 200 } K\in\{4,10,25,50,100,200\} . The two conditions are therefore not pool-matched: LC evaluates reading and evidence utilization when all gold source articles are guaranteed present, whereas RAG must first retrieve the required evidence from the full corpus. Accordingly, this experiment diagnoses the contribution of open-corpus retrieval failures to end-to-end performance; it is not a direct LC–RAG comparison under identical candidate pools. In both conditions, gold facts are re-mapped to line numbers inside the assembled context; in RAG, a gold fact that is not retrieved has no corresponding gold line. Appendix D reports the corresponding retrieval ceilings (Hits@ k k for any vs. all gold facts) and reproduces the answer-only RAG baselines from the original paper.

sections.heading: QASPER-MP .
sections.text: QASPER ( Dasigi et al., 2021 ) contains 5,049 information-seeking questions over 1,585 NLP papers, each annotated by domain experts with paragraph-level evidence and a short free-form or extractive answer (including Unanswerable ). The original task is single-document and, therefore, does not exercise the retrieval pipeline. We construct QASPER-MP (multi-paper) by pairing each gold paper with ten distractor papers sampled from the QASPER pool, yielding an 11-paper haystack per query, and rewrite every question to include a realistic paper cue - in ∼ \sim 50% of cases a first-author surname (e.g., “Smith et al.”), and otherwise a 2–3 word verbatim title fragment - split by a hash of the question id. This forces the system to resolve document identity from a realistic cue rather than the full paper title. The task jointly tests document identification, evidence localization, and answer generation. Since distractors come from the same NLP-paper collection, they provide domain-matched context. A successful system must identify the relevant paper and supporting paragraph(s) before answering, while retaining QASPER’s expert-annotated answers and evidence. For LC, papers are serialized in an XML-like format that preserves titles, abstracts, and section structure ( <paper> , <title> , <abstract> , <section> ); paragraphs are line-numbered, and the same paragraph-level gold labels are used for evidence scoring. For RAG, we evaluate both a flat variant (concatenate the top- K K retrieved paragraphs in rank order) and a structured variant that re-emits the surrounding <paper> / <title> / <abstract> scaffolding and inserts “ ... ” markers for discontinuities, so that retrieved fragments retain their document provenance. We evaluate QASPER-MP at two scales. For proprietary models, we conduct a pilot on N = 50 N{=}50 queries, comprising 38 answerable and 12 unanswerable examples. For open-weight models, we expand the evaluation to N = 200 N{=}200 queries, providing broader benchmark coverage and a more stable estimate of aggregate performance. Because the proprietary-model results are based on the smaller pilot, comparisons across the two model groups should be interpreted with the corresponding difference in sampling uncertainty in mind. Construction details, sampling procedures, prompts, and the LLM-judge protocol are provided in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We organize our experiments around four research questions: • RQ1. What are the practical limitations of RAG, and can long-context EBG address them? • RQ2. Does requiring models to explicitly cite evidence improve answer accuracy? • RQ3. Can models correctly cite evidence lines even in a two-needle setting? • RQ4. Can models remain context-faithful even when evidence contradicts their built-in knowledge?

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We evaluate 10 state-of-the-art proprietary models from three major providers across different experiments: GPT-4o , GPT-4.1 , o3-mini , GPT-5 , GPT-5.5 , Sonnet-4 , Sonnet-4.5 , Opus-4.6 , Gemini-2.5-Fl , and Gemini-3-Fl . Additionally we evaluate three open-weight models served through Fireworks.ai 1 1 1 https://fireworks.ai/ - GPT-OSS-120B , GLM-5.2 , and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B (or Nemo-3.5-L in short) - to test whether our findings hold beyond proprietary systems. We evaluate evidence-based generation ( EBG ) under both long-context ( LC ) and RAG settings. Prompt templates for the answer-only and EBG conditions are provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 5.1.1 Multi-document QA setup.
sections.text: For RQ1 , we use two multi-document QA datasets - MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP . Construction details, retrieval variants, and the LLM-judge protocol are in Appendices D and E .

sections.heading: Synthetic Dataset.
sections.text: We sweep context lengths from 10K to 1M characters. For each length, we run N = 100 N{=}100 trials: each trial draws a fresh distractor haystack and samples one needle uniformly from the 10 curated two-hop needles. Here we apply the answer-only and EBG prompts and report Ans* , Ans , Evid , and Ans+Evid accuracies. A sanity check at L = 10 ​ K L{=}10\text{K} confirms all models achieve ≥ 0.98 {\geq}0.98 joint accuracy, establishing that degradation at longer lengths reflects context handling rather than needle ambiguity. This setup addresses RQ2 and RQ3 ; there are no contradictory needles, so RQ4 is not evaluated here.

sections.heading: NoLiMa-based Dataset.
sections.text: Under the NoLiMa setting, we use B 1 c B^{c}_{1} as the haystack source across all context lengths to maintain a controlled evaluation setup. We use the T01 test variant throughout, as it provides exactly one input argument for the one-hop question and one for the two-hop question associated with each needle. This enables a consistent comparison between direct retrieval and commonsense composition while holding the underlying needle fixed. For example, for 0405 , the one-hop question is instantiated with fish-based meals , whereas the two-hop question uses Brandade ; similarly, 0402 uses milk and a cappuccino , respectively. We test two characters, Yuki and Stuart , at the insertion depths defined in § 4.2 , yielding 16 needle-placement conditions per context length per model (4 needles × \times 4 depths). We evaluate three settings: single-needle (one-hop and two-hop, addressing RQ2 ), two-needle (two-hop with explicit secondary evidence, addressing RQ3 ), and contradictory two-needle (CTN, addressing RQ4 ). Results are reported separately for one-hop and two-hop questions and averaged across the corresponding conditions.

sections.heading: 5.1.3 NoLiMa-based RAG Setup
sections.text: We compare long-context LC and RAG on the NoLiMa-based dataset under RQ1 (Appendix G ). We first analyze RAG retrieval performance for the single-needle and two-needle settings using one-hop and two-hop questions, examining how the retrieval depth required for full evidence coverage changes with haystack length and reasoning complexity. After needle insertion, each haystack line is embedded using OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small model and ranked by cosine similarity to the query. We then compare RAG and LC under the same EBG prompting, reporting Ans accuracy. Since RAG contexts can be smaller than their source haystacks, we use matched character budgets. For each haystack length, we identify the minimum top- k k providing full evidence coverage, compute its character count, and match it to the closest available LC context length. Table 15 summarizes this mapping. For example, full-coverage retrieval from the 1M-character haystack in the two-needle setting requires 920 vectors (217,152 characters) and is matched to the 200K LC condition. This approximately controls for the amount of text presented to the model and isolates retrieval-ranked versus long-context inputs under comparable budgets.

sections.heading: 5.2 Results
sections.text: We report results organized by the research questions introduced in § 5 .

sections.heading: RQ1: LC-EBG addresses two RAG limitations.
sections.text: On MultiHop-RAG , queries require 2–4 evidence facts spread across distinct articles, so faithful answering requires the retriever to surface all required facts within its top- k k budget. For this benchmark, the two conditions use different evidence-access regimes: open-corpus RAG searches 6,296 chunks constructed from all 609 articles , whereas the oracle-containing LC condition receives every gold-evidence article plus 20 distractor articles. The conditions are therefore not pool-matched; this comparison diagnoses the cost of open-corpus retrieval relative to reading when the gold source articles are guaranteed to be available. We first reproduce the answer-only RAG baselines from the original benchmark under our pipeline ( text-embedding-3-large + 256-token windows; Appendix D ) and measure annotated-gold retrieval coverage directly. At k = 10 k{=}10 , the retriever covers any gold fact for 82 % 82\% of queries but covers all gold facts for only 19 % 19\% (and just 8 % 8\% on inference queries). This all-vs-any gap exposes a limitation of the evaluated similarity-retrieval setup: it often retrieves some relevant evidence but fails to recover the complete evidence set required for multi-fact queries within a practical top- k k budget. When the gold annotations are exhaustive and every annotated fact is necessary, all-gold coverage bounds the faithfully grounded performance of the downstream RAG reader. The reader results corroborate this limitation (Appendix D.5 , Table 6 ). Under EBG prompting at k = 10 k{=}10 , open-corpus RAG achieves Ans accuracies of 60 / 48 / 44 % 60/48/44\% for GPT-5 , Sonnet-4.5 , and Gemini-3-Fl , respectively, whereas the oracle-containing LC-EBG condition achieves 86 / 82 / 78 % 86/82/78\% on the same queries. The resulting 26 26 – 34 34 pp gap includes the cost of retrieving the required evidence from the full corpus and should not be interpreted as a pool-matched estimate of an intrinsic LC–RAG difference. The gap remains at k = 200 k{=}200 , where the open-corpus RAG context approaches the size of the LC haystack despite comparable context sizes, but its Ans accuracy remains lower for all three models. Under answer-only prompting, open-corpus RAG at k = 200 k{=}200 reaches parity with the oracle-containing LC condition only for Sonnet-4.5 ( 68 % 68\% vs. 68 % 68\% ). Consistent with this, our NoLiMa -based RAG analysis (Table 13 ) shows that retrieval costs scale sharply with reasoning complexity and haystack length . While one-hop full coverage remains relatively efficient, two-hop retrieval grows from 1.9K retrieved characters at 10K context to over 202K at 1M context, effectively pushing RAG toward brute-force long-context processing without guaranteeing complete evidence recovery. sections.heading: RQ2: Citation improves answer accuracy.
sections.text: On the synthetic benchmark (Fig. 4(a) , Appendix F.1 ), all three frontier models - GPT-5, Claude Sonnet-4.5, and Gemini-3-Flash - approach ceiling answer accuracy under both prompting conditions ( answer-only and EBG ). GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Flash maintain ≥ 98 % \geq 98\% accuracy across all tested context lengths, while Sonnet-4.5 remains within the 93 93 – 100 % 100\% range up to 700K characters. Consequently, the synthetic dataset shows no measurable citation-as-scaffold effect on answer accuracy: Ans ∗ and Ans remain within sampling noise across all cells, including at the longest contexts . This does not refute RQ2 but reflects the controlled benchmark design: lexically dissimilar distractors make the two-hop facts relatively easy to isolate, leaving little headroom for EBG’s benefits. A different pattern emerges on the more challenging NoLiMa-based LC benchmark (Fig. 1 ), where the scaffolding effect becomes apparent under long-context stress . Sonnet and Gemini models gain between + 9 +9 and + 19 +19 pp from EBG prompting across context lengths from 300K to 900K. Among open-weight models, the smaller Nemo-3.5-L improves by + 3 +3 to + 12 +12 pp, while GLM-5.2 reaches a maximum gain of + 16 +16 pp at 700K; in contrast, GPT-OSS-120B shows no benefit. Taken together, the contrast between the synthetic and NoLiMa settings suggests that scaffolding is most useful when long-context retrieval is sufficiently challenging, while its effectiveness remains model-dependent and may not simply scale with model capacity .

sections.heading: RQ3: Asymmetric Retrieval Behavior.
sections.text: Figure 2: Two-needle citation breakdown: rate of correctly citing the primary needle vs. the secondary needle under NoLiMa-based LC benchmark. Higher ( ↑ \uparrow ) values are better. As shown in Fig. 2 , recovery of the two evidence types varies substantially across models. Gemini-3-Fl and GPT-5 achieve near-perfect and balanced citation of both the primary and secondary needles (99.5/99.8% and 95.1/98.6%, respectively). Gemini-2.5-Fl also performs relatively well, but exhibits an inversion, with secondary-needle citation exceeding primary-needle citation (80.8% vs. 67.4%). A similar, more pronounced inversion appears for o3-mini (88.4% vs. 54.9%). These cases suggest that successful recovery of one evidence type does not necessarily imply comparable recovery of the other. This asymmetry reverses for several other models, where primary-needle recovery substantially exceeds secondary-needle recovery. GPT-4.1 , GPT-4o , and the Sonnet models exhibit this pattern, with the largest disparities observed for GPT-4o (71.3% vs. 20.9%) and Sonnet-4.5 (64.6% vs. 21.4%). This disparity indicates that retrieving the primary evidence does not guarantee successful attribution of the complementary evidence required for the task. Moreover, primary-needle citation itself remains imperfect, showing that retrieval failures extend beyond the secondary signal alone. The open-weight models show substantial variation in retrieval. GLM-5.2 achieves balanced recovery (78.5% primary and 85.2% secondary), whereas GPT-OSS-120B records lower rates for both needles (26.1% and 29.4%). Nemo-3.5-L performs poorly on both (11.8% and 6.5%), indicating broader retrieval limitation rather than directional asymmetry. Overall, multi-evidence retrieval varies across models and evidence types, reinforcing model-dependent patterns as in RQ1. Figure 3: TN vs. CTN , Ans+Evid . TN uses a factual secondary needle; CTN uses a contradictory secondary needle, conflicting with world knowledge, requiring context-faithful reasoning and citation. Models to the right of the dashed line are open-weight. Higher ( ↑ \uparrow ) values are better. Ans accuracy for the same runs is reported in Figure 6 .

sections.heading: RQ4: CTN amplifies failure.
sections.text: Performance generally declines under contradiction, with substantial variation across models (Fig. 3 ); answer accuracy is reported separately in Figure 6 . GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Fl remain relatively context-faithful, preserving high answer accuracy, though their Ans+Evid still drops, indicating greater sensitivity of evidence grounding to contradiction. In contrast, GPT-4.1 , GPT-4o , and the Sonnet variants show sharper declines, particularly in Ans+Evid , suggesting they can recover the expected answer while failing to reconcile contradictory evidence. CTN robustness is also uneven among open-weight models. GLM-5.2 is notably resilient: Ans decreases only from 79% to 72%, while Ans+Evid changes from 73% to 70%, largely preserving the small gap between the two metrics. By contrast, GPT-OSS-120B and Nemo-3.5-L start from substantially weaker TN baselines: the former falls from 28/8% ( Ans / Ans+Evid ) to 8/5% under CTN, and the latter from 12/6% to 5/4%. These models therefore already struggle to extract and ground answers under TN, with CTN further compounding this weakness. Overall, Ans+Evid is generally more vulnerable to CTN than Ans , showing that resolving contradiction while grounding the answer in supplied evidence is harder than producing the correct answer itself. The widening Ans – Ans+Evid gap highlights a common failure mode: models reach the expected answer without faithfully using the context that should justify it, even when answers remain correct. See Appendix F.4 for more details.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: We introduced evidence-based generation (EBG) , a framework that requires models to produce both an answer and line-level citations, together with a joint Ans+Evid metric that measures correctness and grounding simultaneously. By separating retrieval from evidence-grounded reasoning, EBG exposes failures obscured by answer-only evaluation. We evaluate these failures using evidence-grounded versions of MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP , a controlled synthetic two-hop haystack, and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K–1M characters. This evaluation suite spans both realistic and controlled settings, allowing retrieval, reasoning, and grounding errors to be examined under complementary conditions. Across ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs, EBG reveals two key RAG limitations: (i) similarity retrieval finds any relevant chunk more reliably than all evidence required for multi-fact queries, imposing a retrieval ceiling at realistic top- k k budgets; and (ii) chunking can discard document-level meta-information needed by identity-bearing queries, causing RAG to over-refuse on retrieval misses. EBG further exposes grounding failures hidden by answer-only metrics: models often cite incomplete evidence, and the gap between answer and joint accuracy widens when in-context evidence conflicts with parametric knowledge. These findings show that correct answers alone can substantially overstate a model’s ability to faithfully use long-context evidence. They also highlight evidence attribution as a useful diagnostic for distinguishing retrieval limitations from downstream reasoning failures. Consequently, EBG provides a more informative basis for comparing RAG and long-context systems than evaluations that collapse retrieval, reasoning, and attribution into answer accuracy alone. These results do not imply that “LC replaces RAG”; rather, LC and RAG exhibit distinct failure modes that EBG helps localize, motivating evaluations that measure both answer accuracy and evidence fidelity. The appropriate architecture may therefore depend not only on answer quality, but also on which sources of failure are acceptable for a given task and context regime. Future work includes scaling EBG to the full benchmarks and testing document-aware chunking. Richer evidence attribution and the observed reasoning benefits of evidence generation also motivate investigating grounding objectives as part of model training.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Our evaluation focuses on synthetic and semi-synthetic long-context benchmarks designed to isolate grounding and evidence attribution behavior under controlled conditions. While these settings enable precise analysis, they do not capture the full complexity of real-world domains such as legal, scientific, or medical reasoning. In addition, our evidence metric operates at the line level and therefore measures coarse-grained provenance rather than fine-grained span-level attribution. The benchmarks also assume that the reference evidence is sufficiently complete and unambiguous, whereas real-world questions may admit multiple valid evidence sets or interpretations. Our RAG analysis estimates end-to-end performance through a decomposition of retrieval and long-context accuracy rather than exhaustive evaluation of full production RAG pipelines across all configurations. We therefore do not systematically explore retrieval variants such as query rewriting, hybrid search, or adaptive context selection, which could alter the observed retrieval ceilings. Finally, because we evaluate proprietary frontier and open-weight models through API access, results may vary as deployed systems evolve over time.

sections.heading: Ethics and Broader Impact
sections.text: This work studies evidence grounding and provenance in long-context language models. Our benchmarks are constructed from synthetic or publicly available text and do not contain sensitive personal information. We do not train new foundation models; all experiments are conducted through inference-only evaluation of existing systems. We believe evidence-based evaluation can improve transparency and verifiability in LLM-based systems by encouraging models to explicitly identify the context used to support their answers. Such capabilities may be particularly important in high-stakes applications such as legal analysis, scientific search, and medical document understanding, where unsupported or hallucinated answers can have significant consequences. At the same time, citation generation should not be interpreted as a guarantee of faithful reasoning. A model may cite irrelevant or incomplete evidence while producing a plausible answer. We therefore view evidence-based generation as a complementary framework rather than a complete solution to factuality or interpretability in language models.

sections.heading: Appendix A Prompt Templates
sections.text: The haystack is line-numbered ( [1] , [2] , …, [N] ) and substituted into the haystack placeholder of each task template. We use four prompt variants: an answer-only variant (no system prompt), a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) variant (no system prompt), an evidence-based generation (EBG) variant that asks the model to cite supporting line numbers in JSON, and a CoT-based EBG variant (no system prompt) that requests both brief reasoning and the EBG JSON answer-and-evidence output. Answer-only Prompt (User Message) You will answer a question based on the following book snippet: {haystack} Use the information provided in the book snippet to answer the question. Your answer should be short and based on either explicitly stated facts or strong, logical inferences. Question: {question} Return only the final answer with no additional explanation or reasoning. CoT Prompt (User Message) You will answer a question based on the following book snippet: {haystack} Use the information provided in the book snippet to answer the question. Be aware that some details may not be stated directly, and you may need to INFER the answer based on the given information. Begin with a brief explanation of your reasoning in NO MORE THAN THREE (3) sentences. Then, return the final answer on a new line. Question: {question} EBG System Prompt Your job is to answer the question entirely from the context and provide a reference. Your answer should cite all lines the answer is based on. EBG User Prompt <context>{haystack}</context> Answer the question based on information only from the context. If the question is not answerable from the context, answer NA. Your response should comprise only the answer and all lines the answer is based on in json format. For example: ```json { ‘‘lines’’: [25, 412], ‘‘answer’’: ‘‘John’’ } ``` Question: {question} CoT-based EBG Prompt (User Message) You will answer a question based on the following book snippet: <context>{haystack}</context> Use the information provided in the book snippet to answer the question. Be aware that some details may not be stated directly, and you may need to INFER the answer based on the given information. Begin with a brief explanation of your reasoning in NO MORE THAN THREE (3) sentences. Then, answer the question based on information only from the context. If the question is not answerable from the context, answer NA. Provide the answer (just the character name) and all lines the answer is based on in json format. For example: ```json { ‘‘lines’’: [25, 412], ‘‘answer’’: ‘‘John’’ } ``` Question: {question}

sections.heading: Appendix B Additional Details of Synthetic Dataset
sections.text: We provide additional details on the construction and structure of our synthetic dataset and present a representative example to illustrate the resulting task format and evidence organization.

sections.heading: B.1 Example
sections.text: Consider facts “Himalaya Inc. launched FitBand” and “Himalaya Inc. is based in Mumbai” , with question “Which smart wearable was launched by a company based in Mumbai?” At L = 10 ​ K L{=}10\text{K} the two facts land at lines 56 and 67 among random distractors: Haystack excerpt and question (synthetic dataset) … 54: Tech research group DataSynergy optimized machine learning algorithms. 55: A renowned sculptor in Rome crafted a public monument. 56: Himalaya Inc. launched a new smart wearable called FitBand. 57: A notable charity, WarmHearts, distributed winter supplies to families in need. 58: GreenWave unveiled a new system for harnessing tidal energy. … 65: Fitness startup VitalMotion developed smart workout equipment. 66: GlobalVoyager published a feature on little-known cultural festivals. 67: Himalaya Inc. is based in Mumbai. 68: Director James Park released a documentary on endangered rainforests. 69: Education reformist Tara Singh promoted progressive teaching methods. … Question: Which smart wearable was launched by a company based in Mumbai? Neither line alone is sufficient: line 56 identifies the product but not the company location, while line 67 identifies the location but not the product. The model must therefore compose evidence across both lines. Under the EBG prompt template, the expected output is a JSON object containing both the answer and the cited line numbers: Expected EBG response { ‘‘lines’’: [56, 67], ‘‘answer’’: ‘‘FitBand’’ } Variant Needle Template Original NoLiMa primary needles (under SN) 0402 “A message came in from { CHAR } saying, ‘I’m lactose intolerant,’ and nothing more.” 0402Inv “A message came in saying, ‘I’m lactose intolerant,’ from { CHAR } .” 0405 “Then { CHAR } mentioned that he has been vegan for years.” 0405Inv “There was a vegan guest, named { CHAR } .” Gender neutral rephrased primary needle (under SN) 0405-R “Then { CHAR } mentioned being vegan for years.” Explicit secondary needles (under TN) TN-0402-S “ { CHAR } said, ‘Cappuccino is a classic Italian coffee made with espresso and steamed milk.’ ” TN-0405-S “Then { CHAR } mentioned that Brandade is a fish-based dish made with salted cod.” Explicit secondary needle (under CTN) CTN-0402-S “Black coffee is a rich and creamy beverage made by brewing coffee beans in steamed whole milk.” CTN-0405-S “Falafel is a popular Middle Eastern dish made from ground chickpeas mixed with minced lamb.” Table 2: Needle templates used in the evaluation. Original NoLiMa needles under the single-needle ( SN ) setting evaluate both one-hop and two-hop reasoning. We add 0405-R , a gender-neutral rephrased version of the 0405 primary needle template under SN, to examine the influence of gendered wording in the needle template. Explicit secondary needles under the two-needle ( TN ) setting directly provide the required world-knowledge fact and evaluate two-hop reasoning under fully contextualized evidence. The contradictory two-needle ( CTN ) setting instead introduces secondary needles that conflict with world knowledge, enabling evaluation of whether models remain strictly faithful to the provided context during two-hop reasoning. Such a response is scored as correct on Ans , Evid , and Ans+Evid . The remaining nine needles follow the same structure with varied entities, relations, and answer forms.

sections.heading: C.1 Needle settings
sections.text: Table 2 presents the different needle templates used across different settings.

sections.heading: C.2 Single Needle (SN) setting
sections.text: In this setting, 0402 and 0402Inv encode the same dietary fact about a character ( {CHAR} ) using different surface forms with altered word order. We refer to the first variant as the default form and the second as the inverse form. Similarly, needles 0405 and 0405Inv state that a character ( {CHAR} ) is vegan . These needles support both one-hop questions answerable directly from the needle (e.g., “ Which character is lactose intolerant?” ) and two-hop questions requiring an additional world-knowledge inference (e.g., “ Which character cannot drink a cappuccino?” , which requires knowing that cappuccino contains milk ). The SN context supplies the entity-specific primary needle but not the complete inference chain required by the question. For example, a needle stating that a character is vegan must be combined with parametric commonsense knowledge that veganism excludes eating fish. We therefore refer to the cited primary needle in SN as anchor evidence . For SN, evidence accuracy measures whether the model cites the correct contextual anchor, and joint accuracy measures answer correctness together with anchor citation; these metrics should not be interpreted as establishing a complete context-only evidence chain. This distinction is specific to SN because part of the information required to answer the query may reside in the model’s parametric knowledge. Accordingly, SN citations cannot directly attribute the contribution of such internally stored information.

sections.heading: C.3 Two-needle (TN) setting
sections.text: As shown in Table 2 , we introduce two explicit secondary needles under the two-needle ( TN ) setting: TN-0402-S and TN-0405-S . These needles explicitly provide the world-knowledge fact required for two-hop reasoning (e.g., “CHAR said, ‘Cappuccino is a classic Italian coffee made with espresso and steamed milk.’,” ). Each secondary needle pairs with the corresponding primary needles. For example, TN-0402-S pairs with 0402 and 0402Inv , while TN-0405-S pairs with 0405 and 0405Inv . Answering a two-hop question, therefore, requires retrieving and jointly reasoning over both the primary and secondary needles.

sections.heading: C.4 Contradictory Two-needle (CTN) setting
sections.text: This setting introduces secondary needles that conflict with world knowledge. For example, CTN-0402-S claims that black coffee contains steamed milk , while CTN-0405-S claims that falafel contains minced lamb . As in TN , each secondary needle pairs with its primary needles (e.g., CTN-0402-S with 0402 and 0402Inv ), testing whether models follow provided context or override it with parametric knowledge. For both question types, the primary needle provides an entity-specific anchor while inference requires unstated bridge knowledge. One-hop questions require a commonsense bridge (e.g., veganism implies avoiding fish), while two-hop questions require an item-composition bridge (e.g., Brandade is fish-based).

sections.heading: Appendix D Long-context EBG vs. RAG on MultiHop-RAG
sections.text: This appendix analyzes an oracle-containing long-context (LC) reading condition and an open-corpus retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) condition on the MultiHop-RAG benchmark ( Tang and Yang, 2024 ) . The LC condition guarantees that every gold-evidence article is available to the reader together with 20 distractor articles, whereas the RAG condition must retrieve the required evidence from the full 609-article corpus. The purpose of this comparison is therefore to diagnose the contribution of open-corpus retrieval failures to end-to-end performance; it is not a pool-matched comparison of LC and RAG under identical candidate document sets. The motivation is direct: our synthetic two-hop benchmark and the NoLiMa-adapted benchmark are constructed haystacks, which leaves open the question of whether the trends we observe carry over to realistic, web-derived multi-document QA where RAG is the natural baseline. The filtered MultiHop-RAG subset (§ 4.3 ) of 2,255 queries tests both EBG (line-level evidence) and RAG (chunked corpus). We run experiments on a 50-query pilot set, sampled with seed 0 and stratified across three types: n inf = 13 n_{\mathrm{inf}}{=}13 , n comp = 21 n_{\mathrm{comp}}{=}21 , and n temp = 16 n_{\mathrm{temp}}{=}16 . We use the same queries, prompts, and scoring throughout, while LC and RAG differ in candidate-document pools as described below.

sections.heading: LC haystacks.
sections.text: For each query, we assemble a mini-haystack of (i) all gold-evidence documents and (ii) 20 distractor documents sampled without replacement from the remaining corpus. Documents are randomly concatenated, split into sentence-level lines, and rendered in the lineno: text format used by our synthetic benchmark. Gold evidence facts are re-mapped to line numbers so EBG labels match the prompt. Mini-haystacks average ∼ 241 \sim 241 K characters ( ∼ 58 \sim 58 K tokens), within every model’s context window. This is the LC (full) condition.

sections.heading: RAG haystacks.
sections.text: For each query, we construct RAG contexts at K ∈ 4 , 10 , 25 , 50 , 100 , 200 K\in{4,10,25,50,100,200} . The retriever searches the full 609-document corpus, divided into 256-token sliding windows (6,296 chunks). We embed chunks and queries with text-embedding-3-large , rank by cosine similarity, and use the top- K K chunks as the RAG context. Each chunk is prefixed with [CHUNK <rank> | <title>] , and rendered with the same sentence-per-line numbering as LC. Gold evidence facts are re-mapped to lines in the retrieved context; unretrieved facts have no corresponding gold line. The conditions are not pool-matched: LC has all gold source articles plus 20 distractors, whereas RAG must locate the required evidence across all 609 articles. This design deliberately preserves the native evidence-access setting of each approach in practice, enabling a realistic comparison between them under their respective retrieval assumptions.

sections.heading: Prompt modes.
sections.text: Each (query, context) pair is evaluated under two prompts differing in one sentence: • Answer-only ( Ans ∗ \texttt{Ans}^{*} ). The model returns a JSON object with only an answer field. We report Ans ∗ \texttt{Ans}^{*} accuracy. • EBG. The model returns a JSON object with answer and lines fields. Scoring uses Ans (string match against the gold answer), Evid,(strict) (every gold line appears in the prediction), and Joint ≡ \equiv Ans+Evid,(strict) (answer-and-evidence). Both prompts share the same system message, instructions, and JSON example template, modulo the citation field. The system message and prompt templates are reproduced verbatim in our accompanying public code release for full reproducibility.

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: We evaluate three frontier LLMs whose context windows comfortably fit under the LC condition: GPT-5 , Sonnet-4.5 , and Gemini-3-Fl . All calls use temperature 0 (or provider equivalent), default sampling parameters, and parallel=5 . This setup keeps decoding conditions consistent across models and experiments.

sections.heading: Scoring.
sections.text: Ans matches the model’s answer string against the gold answer using the same normalization used in the synthetic and NoLiMa experiments. Evid (strict) requires the predicted line-id set to contain every gold line for that query; partial matches are scored separately as Evid (recall) but only Evid (strict) is used for Joint . API failures (timeouts, safety refusals, transient connection errors) are excluded from the denominator; in practice this affected at most one cell (Sonnet-4.5, RAG @200 EBG , n = 49 / 50 n{=}49/50 ). Thus, reported scores reflect successfully completed model calls only.

sections.heading: D.2 Experiment A: Long-context EBG on MultiHop-RAG
sections.text: We run the LC condition to establish base rates and test RQ2 ( Does requiring explicitly citing evidence improve answer accuracy? ) on a non-synthetic benchmark. Each model sees the full mini-haystack ( ∼ 241 \sim 241 K characters) and is prompted in answer-only or EBG mode. Table 3 summarizes results. sections.heading: Answer accuracy: oracle-containing LC exceeds open-corpus RAG under the evaluated budgets.
sections.text: Across both prompts and all three models, oracle-containing LC outperforms open-corpus RAG for K ≤ 100 K\leq 100 . At K = 200 K{=}200 , with 96% gold-fact recall and 90% all-needles coverage, RAG ties LC for Sonnet-4.5 ( 68 % 68\% ) but remains 4,pp below for GPT-5 ( 78 % 78\% vs. 82 % 82\% ) and 10,pp below for Gemini-3-Flash ( 70 % 70\% vs. 80 % 80\% ). At K = 10 K{=}10 , the LC–RAG gap is 22 22 – 44 44 ,pp under answer-only prompting and 26 26 – 34 34 ,pp under EBG. These gaps include full-corpus retrieval and thus compare open-corpus RAG with evidence-guaranteed LC, not an intrinsic LC advantage under identical candidate pools.

sections.heading: Strict evidence: small- K K RAG and LC are comparable.
sections.text: Evid (strict) is roughly flat across K K for each model (10–40% absolute), with no clean monotone trend. This reflects two distinct requirements for evidence correctness: all needles must be retrieved (coverage, Table 5 ) and the model must cite all of them correctly (citation behaviour). Small K K favors the latter because the citation surface is limited, whereas large K K favors the former as retrieval coverage improves. Increasing K K therefore trades easier citation selection for greater evidence availability, and these opposing effects roughly cancel. Consequently, small- K K RAG can remain comparable to LC on strict evidence despite substantially lower retrieval coverage.

sections.heading: Joint (faithful) accuracy: mixed.
sections.text: Joint = Ans ∧ \wedge Evid (also written as Ans+Evid ) is the most diagnostic number. Two trends are visible. First, joint decreases with K K for every model: at large K K the citation surface grows, the model loses track of which retrieved chunk it used, and joint collapses despite the higher answer recall. Second, the best RAG joint is always at small K K ( K = 4 K{=}4 for all three models), where the citation problem is trivial and the only queries that score are the ones whose needles happened to be in the top 4 (14% of queries). Aggregate joint therefore over-rewards a regime that only works on the easy fraction of queries. LC’s joint sits at 28%, 8%, 28% - competitive with RAG@4 for GPT-5 and Gemini, behind for Sonnet - and is computed over the full pilot set rather than the small subset where retrieval succeeded.

sections.heading: D.6 Discussion
sections.text: We highlight four takeaways for the manuscript.

sections.heading:
Takeaway 1: LC EBG dominates RAG for answer accuracy, at every
realistic retrieval budget.
sections.text: Under the answer-only prompt, the oracle-containing LC condition exceeds open-corpus RAG@10 by 22 22 – 44 44 pp and exceeds RAG@200 by 0 0 – 10 10 pp. The same qualitative pattern holds under EBG. Because the two conditions do not share a candidate-document pool, these numbers quantify the combined cost of document discovery and passage retrieval relative to evidence-guaranteed reading; they are not a pool-matched estimate of an architecture-level LC–RAG effect.

sections.heading:
Takeaway 2: RAG’s retrieval bottleneck is multi-hop coverage,
not single-hop recall.
sections.text: Hits@10 (any gold) is 82% but Hits@10 (all gold) is only 19% (Table 4 ); on inference queries the all-gold number falls to 8%. The principal source of the observed gap relative to the oracle-containing LC control is that, at small K K , open-corpus RAG rarely retrieves the complete union of annotated gold facts.

sections.heading:
Takeaway 3: Citations as a reasoning scaffold replicate
outside the synthetic setting.
sections.text: Ans accuracy under EBG is higher than under the answer-only prompt for two of three models, with a striking + 14 +14 pp improvement for Sonnet-4.5 (Table 3 ). This is the RQ1 effect that was masked on our synthetic benchmark by ceiling performance.

sections.heading: Takeaway 4: The grounding gap is a real-data phenomenon.
sections.text: The Ans − - Joint gap in the LC condition is 50–74 pp depending on model, and is largest on inference queries. Models routinely produce a correct multi-hop answer while citing only one of the two required hops - the same asymmetric-retrieval failure mode we documented on the synthetic benchmark, here observed on naturalistic web data.

sections.heading: D.8 Limitations and next steps
sections.text: The frontier-model experiments use a 50-query pilot, so the reported estimates remain subject to sampling variation, particularly for small question-type slices such as the 13 inference queries. Evaluating all 2,255 usable queries would provide tighter confidence intervals. We also hold the retriever fixed to text-embedding-3-large with 256-token sliding windows. Reranking, hybrid sparse–dense retrieval, query expansion, longer chunks, and document-aware indexing could improve the open-corpus RAG results. For the evaluated retriever, corpus-wide all-gold Hits@ 10 10 is 19 % 19\% over the 2,255 usable queries; on the 50-query pilot, all-gold coverage at K = 10 K{=}10 is 28 % 28\% . Under the assumptions that the gold annotations are exhaustive and that every annotated fact is necessary, these coverage rates strongly constrain faithfully grounded performance at this retrieval budget. A key design limitation is that the MultiHop-RAG LC and RAG conditions are not pool-matched. The LC condition is an oracle-containing reading control : every gold-evidence article is guaranteed to be present together with 20 distractor articles. The RAG condition instead performs open-corpus retrieval over the full 609-article corpus. Consequently, the reported LC–RAG gaps combine the effects of full-corpus document discovery, passage retrieval, and downstream reading; they should not be interpreted as an intrinsic ranking of LC and RAG under matched evidence access. A complementary pool-matched RAG condition that retrieves from the same per-query gold-plus-20 candidate set would separate within-pool chunking and ranking effects from the cost of full-corpus document discovery. We leave this controlled comparison, together with evaluation of stronger retrieval pipelines and the full query set, to future work.

sections.heading: Appendix E Long-context EBG vs. RAG on QASPER-MP
sections.text: This appendix documents a second comparison of long-context evidence-based generation (LC EBG) against retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), this time on a multi-paper adaptation of QASPER ( Dasigi et al., 2021 ) that we call QASPER-MP . Whereas MultiHop-RAG (Appendix D ) tests multi-document reasoning on news, QASPER-MP tests it on scientific papers, where the gold question–answer–evidence triples were written assuming a single known paper. To make the task non-trivial under retrieval, we (i) place each gold paper alongside ten distractor papers, (ii) rewrite the question so it identifies the target paper by a realistic short reference (an author name or a 2–3 word topic cue), and (iii) evaluate in both LC and RAG conditions over the same 50-query stratified pilot. The headline finding is that the aggregate score (Answer-F1 or LLM-judge, averaged over all questions) makes LC and RAG look roughly tied, but this tie hides an answerability asymmetry: LC EBG beats RAG by 5–22 judge points on answerable questions for every frontier model tested , while RAG “wins” on unanswerable questions because it over-refuses. The over-refusal mechanically matches the QASPER Unanswerable gold label on the 24% of pilot questions where that is the correct answer, pulling the aggregate up.

sections.heading: Dataset.
sections.text: We use the QASPER dev split ( N = 1,005 N=1{,}005 questions over 281 papers). Each question is annotated with an answer type ( extractive , abstractive , boolean , or none - meaning unanswerable from the paper) and an evidence set : the list of paragraphs from the paper that support the answer. Up to three annotators contribute per question; we follow the official QASPER evaluator and take the max F1 across annotators.

sections.heading: 50-query pilot.
sections.text: We sample 50 questions, stratified by answer type, so that the composition matches the dev-split distribution: 13 boolean, 13 abstractive, 12 extractive, 12 unanswerable. This split (38 answerable, 12 unanswerable) is the denominator for every condition below.

sections.heading: Multi-paper haystacks (LC condition).
sections.text: For each pilot query we build an 11-paper haystack consisting of the gold paper plus 10 distractor papers drawn uniformly from the dev split. Each paper is rendered with explicit document boundaries: <paper> <title> Paper title </title> <abstract> Paper abstract </abstract> <section> Section name </section> Paragraph 1 of that section Paragraph 2 of that section … </paper> Lines are concatenated and numbered i: <line> so the model can cite specific lines as evidence (consistent with our EBG protocol). The median LC haystack size is ∼ \sim 32K characters; the largest is ∼ \sim 56K. The gold-evidence paragraph(s) for each query are re-mapped to line indices in the assembled haystack.

sections.heading: RAG condition.
sections.text: We embed every QASPER dev paragraph and every (disambiguated) query with OpenAI text-embedding-3-large , and retrieve the top- K K paragraphs by cosine similarity. We evaluate four retrieval variants, factored as { flat , struct } × { pool11 , full } \{\text{flat},\,\text{struct}\}\times\{\text{pool11},\,\text{full}\} : flat_pool11. Top- K K paragraphs retrieved from the same 11-paper pool as the LC haystack (pool-matched candidate corpus). The reader sees a flat list of retrieved paragraphs with a one-line [CHUNK <rank> | <title>] marker before each. struct_pool11. Same retrieval, but paragraphs are regrouped by their source paper and wrapped in the same XML layout used for LC. Within a paper, paragraphs are sorted by their original index, and discontinuities (gaps where intermediate paragraphs were not retrieved) are marked with a single ... line. flat_full / struct_full. Same as above but retrieving from the full dev corpus ( N ≈ 6,000 N\approx 6{,}000 paragraphs) rather than the 11-paper pool. This is the realistic open-corpus RAG setting: the retriever must locate the target paper among hundreds of similar NLP papers using only the short cue in the rewritten question.

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: We evaluate five frontier reasoning models: GPT-5 , GPT-5.5 , Claude Opus 4.6 , Claude Sonnet 4.5 , and Gemini 3 Flash (preview). All runs use the same query set, the same retrieval indices, and the same EBG prompt template. Citation rules in the prompt forbid citing structural lines ( <title> , <abstract> , <paper> , [CHUNK , or ... ); these lines are present only as context.

sections.heading: Question disambiguation.
sections.text: QASPER questions were written to be unambiguous given the paper; many become ambiguous in a multi-paper haystack (e.g., “What evaluation metrics were used?” becomes pathological with 11 candidate papers). We disambiguate each pilot question by inserting a short paper cue , chosen deterministically 50/50 from two cue types: • Author cue ( n = 24 n=24 ): “In Smith et al., …” , with surname(s) drawn from the arXiv metadata of the gold paper. Conventions: 1 author → \to “Smith” , 2 authors → \to “Smith and Doe” , ≥ 3 \geq 3 authors → \to “Smith et al.” . • Title cue ( n = 26 n=26 ): “In the ⟨ \langle cue ⟩ \rangle paper, …” , where the cue is a verbatim 2–3 word substring of the paper title (e.g., “Vietnamese Word Segmentation” , “Winograd Schemas” , “TF-IDF Features” ). Cues are intentionally short and realistic, matching what a researcher would type into a search box. This makes the retrieval problem genuinely harder than indexing on full titles or descriptive paraphrases.

The aggregate score thus rewards RAG’s high refusal rate. Once we condition on answerability, the LC > > RAG gap on actually answerable questions is consistent across models and retrieval variants.

sections.heading: E.3 Disambiguation Details and Cue Length Sensitivity
sections.text: We initially experimented with longer “descriptive” cues generated by GPT-5 from each paper’s title and abstract (e.g., “In the cross-lingual zero-shot NMT paper” ). These cues are unrealistically informative: they often include domain phrases that do not appear in the title at all, which makes retrieval implausibly easy. Embedding-based retrieval coverage with descriptive cues was 60.0% (all-needles@10, full corpus). Switching to the short, realistic cues described in Appendix E.1 dropped coverage to 48.0% - a 12-point hit - reflecting the fact that “In Smith et al.” or “In the BERTSUM paper” is a much weaker retrieval signal than a paraphrased domain summary. We use the short, realistic cues throughout this appendix because they correspond to how researchers actually query systems in practice; the + + 12pp coverage gain on descriptive cues would inflate RAG numbers relative to what users would experience.

sections.heading: E.4 Structured RAG, Citation Eligibility, and Discontinuity Markers
sections.text: A first iteration of structured RAG produced a counterintuitive result: struct_pool11@3 underperformed flat_pool11@3 on Evidence-F1 across models (gaps of 0.07–0.12), despite carrying more information than the flat baseline (abstract per paper). On inspection, ∼ \sim 44% of structured-RAG citations pointed at <title> or <abstract> lines: when an abstract paraphrases the answer, the model cites it - but QASPER gold evidence excludes abstracts, so abstract citations cannot match gold. We therefore made two changes to the structured layout and prompt used throughout the main results: 1. Citation eligibility. The EBG prompt forbids citing structural lines ( <title> , <abstract> , <paper> , </paper> , [CHUNK , and ... ). Models must cite at least one body paragraph line for any non-refusal answer. Titles and abstracts remain visible as context; they are simply not valid evidence. 2. Discontinuity markers. Within each paper, retrieved paragraphs are sorted by their original paragraph index, and any gap (the abstract followed by paragraph 2, or paragraph 5 followed by paragraph 9) is marked with a single ... line. This gives the reader explicit signal that some material is missing between the visible paragraphs. Under this revised protocol (Table 8 ), structured RAG recovers: Evidence-F1 jumps by + + 0.04 to + + 0.15 per model and struct_pool11@3 beats or matches flat_pool11@3 for two of five models. The intuition that paper-level structure is useful is correct - it had been masked by a metric artifact.

sections.heading: E.5 LLM-Judge Evaluation
sections.text: To control for token-F1 brittleness on paraphrases, we additionally score outputs with an LLM judge: • Judge model: GPT-5. • Inputs: the original question, all annotator gold answers, and the model prediction. • Output: a single number in { 0 , 0.5 , 1 } \{0,\,0.5,\,1\} . The judge is instructed to be lenient about formatting and elaboration but strict about content; partial credit (0.5) is reserved for answers that capture some but not all required information. “Unanswerable” vs. “Unanswerable” scores 1.0; “Unanswerable” vs. a real answer (or the reverse) scores 0.0. Judgments are cached by content hash so repeated scoring is free. Across all conditions, Judge scores are systematically higher than Answer-F1 (the judge is lenient about phrasing), but the ordering of conditions is preserved. The LC vs. RAG gap on answerable questions is larger under the judge than under Answer-F1, because the judge does not penalize Sonnet-4.5 and Gemini-3-Flash for their characteristic boolean elaborations.

sections.heading: E.7 Strengthening RAG: metadata-in-chunk retrieval
sections.text: The full-corpus RAG deficit above is partly a retrieval failure rather than solely a limitation of the downstream reader. After v2 disambiguation, each query carries only a short, typically 2 2 – 3 3 word cue identifying the relevant paper. In the baseline index, however, candidate chunks are embedded as raw paragraph text, without any explicit representation of document identity. The retriever must therefore infer the connection between a sparse paper-level cue in the query and a paragraph whose local content may never mention the paper title or otherwise reveal its source. This mismatch is especially consequential in the full-corpus setting, where evidence from the gold paper competes with paragraphs drawn from the entire ∼ \sim 281-paper dev corpus. Even when the query contains enough information to identify the intended document, the embedding space has no direct document-level feature with which to exploit that signal, making it easy for the gold paper - and consequently the relevant evidence within it - to fall outside the retrieval budget. A natural way to give RAG a fairer chance is therefore to expose document identity directly to the retriever by injecting metadata into the indexed chunks. We rebuild the retrieval index so that every paragraph is embedded together with its source paper’s title, using the representation “ title \n\n paragraph ”. This modification creates an explicit lexical and semantic bridge between the short paper cue supplied by v2 disambiguation and every paragraph originating from that paper, while preserving the paragraph text needed to rank evidence within the document. We then re-run the hardest retrieval condition, flat_full@10 , at n = 200 n{=}200 for all five readers. Importantly, this intervention is confined to retrieval: generation-side rendering, prompting, context construction, and reader settings are unchanged. Thus, any downstream improvement can be attributed to changing the representation used for ranking rather than to providing the reader with additional metadata or altering the generation procedure. Metadata-in-chunk produces a large improvement in evidence retrieval. On the 200 200 -query set, the fraction of queries for which the full gold-evidence set is recovered within the top- 10 10 increases from 43.5 % 43.5\% to 61.0 % 61.0\% , a gain of 17.5 17.5 percentage points. Gold-paragraph recall rises even more substantially in relative terms, from 30.6 % 30.6\% to 50.3 % 50.3\% ( + 19.7 +19.7 pp). These gains indicate that the original full-corpus deficit was not simply caused by an insufficient top- k k budget: a substantial portion arose because the retriever lacked a representation of the very document-level signal introduced during query disambiguation. Prepending the title allows that signal to influence ranking directly, increasing both the probability that the correct paper is represented among the retrieved chunks and the amount of gold evidence that reaches the reader. The retrieval gains propagate consistently to answer quality (Table 11 ). On the answerable subset, the judge score improves for every model. The four strongest readers - GPT-5, Sonnet-4.5, GPT-OSS-120B, and GLM-5.2 - gain between + 0.10 +0.10 and + 0.13 +0.13 , while Nemotron improves by + 0.03 +0.03 . The answerable-question refusal rate also falls by 5 5 – 8 8 ,pp, consistent with fewer queries reaching the reader with distractor or insufficient context. That the same retrieval-only intervention benefits readers with different capabilities strengthens the interpretation that evidence availability is a shared bottleneck across otherwise diverse reader architectures and levels of baseline answer quality. Part of the reader-level degradation under full-corpus RAG is therefore upstream: when document identity is represented during retrieval, more evidence survives the top- 10 10 bottleneck, giving all five readers a better opportunity to answer.
