sections.heading: E.8 Summary
sections.text: QASPER-MP corroborates the picture in Appendix D : under the pool-matched pool11 condition, long-context EBG and RAG end up at comparable aggregate scores, but the mechanism is asymmetric. RAG’s higher refusal rate inflates its score on unanswerable questions; on the answerable subset - where retrieval quality actually matters - LC EBG beats every RAG variant for every one of the five frontier models we tested. The gap is largest for the strongest readers (Opus-4.6 and GPT-5.5 each show + 0.13 +0.13 judge points LC over best RAG on answerable questions), suggesting that LC EBG benefits disproportionately from stronger long-context comprehension. The gap widens further when the retrieval corpus expands from the apples-to-apples 11-paper pool to the realistic full-corpus setting, where LC outperforms the best RAG configuration by 5–13 judge points.

sections.heading: Appendix F Long-context EBG: Synthetic and NoLiMa-based Datasets
sections.text: This appendix collects the controlled long-context EBG results that support RQ2–RQ4: the synthetic two-hop benchmark (§ F.1 ) and the NoLiMa-based benchmark (§ F.2 ).

sections.heading: Observations.
sections.text: As shown in Table 12 , EBG prompting is more beneficial for multi-hop queries than for simple one-hop queries. In one-hop settings, many strong models already perform near ceiling under answer-only prompting, leaving little room for explicit evidence organization to help. In some cases, the additional structure introduced by EBG even hurts performance, suggesting that it may interfere with models that already perform strong implicit retrieval or that are sensitive to extra reasoning overhead. The benefits of EBG become clearer in the two-hop setting, where models must retrieve and combine evidence across multiple pieces of context. The best long-context performers are GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Fl , but for different reasons. GPT-5 is highly robust regardless of prompting strategy, while Gemini-3-Fl gains substantially from EBG in two-hop settings. The strongest evidence in favor of EBG comes from the Gemini-3-Fl two-hop results, where EBG improves performance consistently across almost all context lengths, including the 1M setting. The Sonnet models also show frequent gains from EBG in two-hop tasks, further supporting the view that explicit evidence organization is most useful when reasoning requires multiple retrieval steps. In contrast, the strongest evidence against universal EBG use comes from GPT-4o , where EBG substantially lowers performance in both one-hop and two-hop tasks. Overall, the table suggests that EBG is especially valuable for long-context multi-hop reasoning in models, but it may be unnecessary for simple one-hop retrieval.

sections.heading: Observations.
sections.text: Fig. 5 reports the combined Ans+Evid accuracy across models, context lengths, and reasoning types. Since this metric requires both the final answer and the supporting evidence to be correct, it is a stricter measure than answer accuracy alone. The results show clear differences in how well models remain both accurate and grounded as context length increases.

sections.heading: One-hop performance.
sections.text: In the one-hop setting, the reported joint Ans+Evid metric measures answer correctness together with citation of the primary contextual anchor, rather than a complete context-only reasoning chain, because for one-hop, part of the inference relies on bridge knowledge not stated in the haystack (such as veganism implying avoidance of fish or lactose intolerance implying avoidance of milk . Here, we observe that most frontier models perform very strongly at short and medium context lengths. GPT-5 , Sonnet-4 , Sonnet-4.5 , Gemini-2.5-Fl , and Gemini-3-Fl frequently achieve near-perfect or perfect accuracy across many context lengths. This suggests that when only one relevant piece of evidence needs to be retrieved, strong long-context models can usually identify the evidence and produce the correct answer reliably. Gemini-3-Fl is the strongest one-hop model overall, maintaining 100% accuracy across all evaluated context lengths, including 1M characters. GPT-5 is also highly robust, achieving 100% accuracy across most context lengths and only dropping slightly to 94% at 1M. Gemini-2.5-Fl also remains strong, although it declines at longer contexts, reaching 81% at 600K and 700K before recovering to 94% at 1M. GPT-4.1 performs well in one-hop reasoning, but its performance decreases at the largest context length, reaching 81% at 1M. GPT-4o and o3-mini show much weaker robustness. GPT-4o drops substantially after 100K characters, while o3-mini degrades sharply beyond 200K characters, falling to 31% at 500K and 19% at 700K.

sections.heading: Two-hop performance.
sections.text: The two-hop setting is significantly harder. Even models that perform very well in one-hop reasoning show larger performance drops when they must retrieve and combine multiple pieces of evidence. This indicates that long-context multi-hop reasoning requires more than simply locating one relevant span; the model must maintain multiple pieces of information and reason over their relationship. Gemini-3-Fl is the strongest model in the two-hop setting. It maintains high accuracy across the context range and achieves 93% at 1M characters. GPT-5 is strong from 10K to 700K, but drops to 81% at 1M. GPT-4.1 performs well through mid-range contexts but declines at 1M, reaching 62%.

sections.heading: F.4 TN vs. CTN on NoLiMa-based Dataset: Adherence to Contextual Evidence
sections.text: We conduct an experiment on the NoLiMa-based dataset to evaluate whether LLMs remain faithful to contextual evidence in two-hop reasoning questions when presented with either factual secondary evidence that aligns with world knowledge ( TN ) or counterfactual secondary evidence that conflicts with world knowledge ( CTN ; e.g., “black coffee has milk”).

sections.heading: Experiment.
sections.text: Under TN and CTN, each query is associated with two needles. We insert the primary needle at the middle of the haystack (depth 0.5 0.5 ) and the secondary needle at one of the sampled depths { 0.0 , 0.33 , 0.67 , 1.0 } \{0.0,0.33,0.67,1.0\} . Since questions must be answered strictly from the provided context, success in CTN requires relying on the contradictory contextual evidence rather than parametric memory. We evaluate the performance of TN and CTN using Ans and Ans+Evid accuracy metrics.

sections.heading: Observations.
sections.text: • Contradiction reliably hurts performance. Averaged across models, CTN reduces Ans accuracy by ≈ \approx 7.0 pp (76.2% → \to 69.2%) and Ans+Evid by ≈ \approx 5.9 pp (49.9% → \to 44.0%). • The Ans+Evid accuracy metric is much harder than Ans. Ans+Evid is far below Ans in both TN and CTN , indicating many correct-answer cases still fail to produce a complete evidence trail. • Robustness varies sharply by model. Gemini-3-Fl and GPT-5 remain most stable; the largest Ans+Evid drops under CTN occur for GPT-4.1 ( ≈ \approx -13 pp ), Gemini-2.5-Fl ( ≈ \approx -10 pp ), and o3-mini ( ≈ \approx -8.6 pp ). • Depth sensitivity persists under contradiction, with the CTN penalty tending to be larger when the secondary needle is deeper, consistent with degraded multi-evidence retrieval under harder placements, i.e., mostly at depths 0.33 and 0.67. • CTN remains below TN across context lengths , indicating contradiction amplifies long-context brittleness as both conditions degrade with length. • Contradiction weakens evidence grounding, not just answers. CTN lowers citation rates for both needles (primary ≈ \approx -7.4 pp and secondary ≈ \approx -4.6 pp ), pointing to provenance failure as a primary failure mode under conflicting information. • The answer dimension degrades too, but less than the joint metric. Figure 6 reports Ans accuracy for the same runs. Every model except Gemini-3-Fl loses answer accuracy under contradiction, with the largest drops for GPT-OSS-120B ( ≈ \approx -17 pp ), Sonnet-4.5 ( ≈ \approx -16 pp ), and Gemini-2.5-Fl and Sonnet-4 ( ≈ \approx -12 pp each). On a model-macro average, CoT improves answer accuracy by approximately 8.5 8.5 pp for one-hop questions and 27.2 27.2 pp for two-hop questions. At the model level, CoT never reduces aggregate one-hop accuracy: it improves accuracy for eight models and matches EBG for GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Fl . The improvements range from 5.9 5.9 pp for GPT-5 to 68.8 68.8 pp for GPT-OSS-120B , with large gains also observed for GLM-5.2 ( + 42.3 +42.3 pp), o3-mini ( + 33.3 +33.3 pp), Gemini-2.5-Fl ( + 31.3 +31.3 pp), and GPT-4o ( + 30.8 +30.8 pp). This larger two-hop effect suggests that explicitly eliciting a short reasoning step is particularly useful when answering requires an additional inference beyond direct needle retrieval. Because vanilla CoT also removes the citation and JSON-output requirements, however, this comparison should be interpreted as a comparison between complete prompting strategies rather than as an isolated estimate of the effect of reasoning alone.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: To examine whether explicit reasoning remains beneficial when evidence citation is retained, we compare standard EBG with CoT-EBG. We report Ans so that this comparison is directly commensurable with the vanilla-CoT comparison in Appendix F.5 , which can only be scored on answer accuracy because the plain CoT prompt requests no citations. Holding the metric fixed across the two experiments isolates the effect of the citation requirement itself. We define Δ = Ans − Ans c ​ e \Delta=\texttt{Ans}-\texttt{Ans}^{ce} , where c ​ e ce denotes CoT-EBG; negative values therefore favor CoT-EBG.

sections.heading: Observations.
sections.text: Fig. 7(b) shows a smaller and more model-dependent effect for one-hop questions. CoT-EBG improves aggregate answer accuracy for five models, matches EBG for two, and lowers it for three, with a model-macro average of 2.2 2.2 pp in favor of CoT-EBG. This mixed result is consistent with the near-ceiling performance of several models on direct one-hop retrieval, where an additional reasoning instruction has limited room to help and may introduce unnecessary output complexity. The two-hop result is more consistent: CoT-EBG improves aggregate Ans accuracy for every evaluated model, by 12.3 12.3 pp on a model-macro average. The gains range from 2.4 2.4 pp for GPT-4.1 to 25.5 25.5 pp for Gemini-2.5-Fl . Substantial improvements are also observed for GPT-OSS-120B and GLM-5.2 ( + 23.6 +23.6 pp each), o3-mini ( + 12.0 +12.0 pp), and Gemini-3-Fl ( + 10.4 +10.4 pp). Thus, explicitly eliciting a brief reasoning step remains beneficial when the evidence-citation requirement and output schema are retained, particularly for multi-hop questions. Taken together, the two experiments suggest that the gains from structured prompting are not attributable to citation formatting alone. Explicit reasoning improves answer accuracy both under vanilla CoT and when the EBG citation requirement is retained, with the largest and most consistent effects appearing in the two-hop setting .

sections.heading: Motivation.
sections.text: During retrieval analysis, we observed that the 0405 needle family requires substantially larger top- k k budgets to achieve reliable retrieval compared to the 0402 family (Figure 8 ). This suggests that retrieval difficulty may be influenced not only by reasoning complexity but also by the surface form of the needle itself . The default 0405 template contains a gendered pronoun: “Then { CHAR } mentioned that he has been vegan for years.” Because the pronoun he is independent of the inserted character name, it may introduce additional semantic signals in the embedding representation that are not directly relevant to the query.

sections.heading: Character sensitivity analysis.
sections.text: To investigate this effect, we compute cosine similarity between the query embedding and needle sentences instantiated with different character names drawn from the NoLiMa corpus. Figure 9 shows the top retrieved variants of the needle and their similarity scores for the query “Which character cannot eat Brandade?” . Figure 9: Ranking of the 0405 needle instantiated with 10 different character names based on cosine similarity to a one-hop test query. Although the sentence semantics remain unchanged, similarity scores vary across character tokens. Higher ( ↑ \uparrow ) values are better. Although the sentence semantics remain unchanged, we observe noticeable variation in similarity scores across character substitutions. This indicates that character tokens themselves influence the embedding representation and can affect retrieval ranking.

sections.heading: Effect of pronoun removal.
sections.text: To isolate the role of the gendered pronoun, we construct a rephrased variant of the needle ( 0405-R , Table 2 ) that removes the pronoun while preserving the meaning: “Then { CHAR } mentioned being vegan for years.” We recompute similarity scores for both the original and rephrased needles across multiple character substitutions. Figure 10 compares cosine similarity between the two formulations. Figure 10: Cosine similarity comparison between the original 0405 needle and the rephrased 0405-R variant across 10 characters . Removing the pronoun consistently increases similarity scores across different characters. Higher positive difference ( ↑ \uparrow ) indicates greater effectiveness of the rephrased version compared to the original. Across most characters, the rephrased template yields slightly higher similarity scores. While the improvement is modest for individual instances, it is systematic across characters, suggesting that removing the pronoun reduces semantic noise in the embedding space.

sections.heading: Implications for RAG retrieval.
sections.text: These results help explain the higher retrieval budget required for the 0405 needle family observed earlier. When the needle contains additional syntactic elements that are not directly aligned with the query semantics, embedding similarity becomes less discriminative. In large haystacks, even small similarity differences can significantly affect ranking, pushing the correct needle lower in the retrieval list and increasing the required top- k k budget. sections.heading: G.3 Retrieval Analysis under Embedding, BM25, and Reranker-RAG Pipelines
sections.text: Motivated by the results and observations in Table 13 , we further investigate whether the observed retrieval bottleneck is specific to embedding-based semantic retrieval or persists across alternative retrieval and ranking strategies.

sections.heading: Setup of Embedding-RAG.
sections.text: We first consider the embedding-based RAG pipeline from the preceding experiment (§ 5.1.3 ), restricting the evaluation to Book 1 ( B 1 c B^{c}_{1} ). The pipeline follows the same retrieval setup as before: the haystack is divided into chunks, represented using dense vector embeddings, and ranked by semantic similarity to the query. We retain the original chunking, retrieval, and full-coverage evaluation protocol, and report the minimum top- k k required to retrieve all evidence for one-hop and two-hop queries, together with the corresponding retrieved character budget. Thus, the Embedding-RAG results in Table 14 serve as the semantic-retrieval baseline against which Okapi BM25 and Qwen3-Reranker-8B are compared.

sections.heading: Setup of BM25-RAG.
sections.text: To examine whether the retrieval limitations observed with embedding-based RAG are specific to semantic similarity search, we replace the vector embedding-based retriever with Okapi BM25 2 2 2 https://pypi.org/project/rank-bm25/ , a lexical retrieval method based on term matching and term-frequency statistics. We keep the evaluation protocol unchanged and measure the minimum retrieval depth required to achieve full evidence coverage for both one-hop and two-hop queries across increasing NoLiMa context lengths. As in our primary analysis, full coverage is defined as the smallest top- k k for which all required evidence facts are present in the retrieved set for every sample. We report both this retrieval depth and its corresponding character budget in Table 14 .

sections.heading: Setup of Reranker-based RAG.
sections.text: We further evaluate whether a stronger learned ranking stage can reduce the retrieval depth required for complete evidence coverage. Specifically, we use Qwen3-Reranker-8B , a fine-tuned reranking model, to reorder candidate passages (retrieved by the embedding-based RAG retriever) according to their relevance to the query. We then evaluate the resulting ranking using the same full-coverage criterion as the BM25-RAG and Embedding-RAG settings. This experiment tests the extent to which a learned reranker can move required evidence toward the top of the ranking and consequently reduce the context passed to the downstream model.

sections.heading: Observations.
sections.text: We observe that BM25-RAG consistently requires substantially larger retrieval budgets than Embedding-RAG, with the difference becoming more pronounced as context length increases. At 1M characters, full coverage of one-hop queries requires 307 vectors (102,475 characters) with BM25-RAG, compared with 104 vectors (23,589 characters) for Embedding-RAG. The same pattern holds for two-hop queries, where BM25-RAG requires 1,061 vectors (265,785 characters), compared with 920 vectors (217,152 characters) for Embedding-RAG. Thus, replacing semantic retrieval with Okapi BM25 does not remove the full-coverage bottleneck; instead, lexical retrieval generally requires retrieving more of the haystack to guarantee that all necessary evidence is available. This gap suggests that semantic similarity provides a stronger ranking signal for isolating relevant evidence as the distractor pool expands. Moreover, the persistent two-hop overhead across both retrievers indicates that jointly recovering multiple evidence pieces remains intrinsically more demanding than single-evidence retrieval. As shown in Table 14 , Qwen3-Reranker-8B improves retrieval efficiency over BM25-RAG and Embedding-RAG. For one-hop queries, evidence ranks first across all context lengths, yielding full coverage at top- 1 1 with 62 characters. For two-hop queries, depth grows with context length: at 1M characters, Reranker-RAG reaches full coverage with 149 vectors (21,372 characters), compared with 920 vectors (217,152 characters) for Embedding-RAG and 1,061 vectors (265,785 characters) for BM25-RAG. Thus, a fine-tuned reranker dramatically reduces the retrieval budget for full evidence coverage. Nevertheless, increasing top- k k for two-hop queries shows that stronger reranking does not eliminate the difficulty of jointly surfacing evidence as the haystack grows. The one-hop–two-hop contrast suggests that evidence multiplicity, not context length alone, drives the remaining burden: joint coverage becomes harder when multiple passages must survive the cutoff.

sections.text: We examine whether LLMs answer more accurately when we give them a randomly sampled long-context haystack or a compact context formed by top- k k ranked retrieval. In the long-context setting, we provide the model with the Book 1 haystack at a target character length and insert the needle at predefined depths. This setting corresponds to randomly sampled haystacks: the long-context construction procedure embeds the relevant evidence within a larger context and determines the surrounding distractors and needle positions. In contrast, the retrieval setting replaces the full randomly sampled haystack with a retrieval-ranked context. For each query, we compute cosine similarity between the query embedding and each chunk embedding in the corresponding vector database, rank all chunks by similarity score, and select the minimum top- k k prefix that contains all gold needle evidence for that condition. We call this value the best top- k k . Because long-context and retrieval inputs differ substantially in structure, we compare them under approximately matched character budgets rather than matched nominal context labels. For each Book 1 haystack, we first compute the total character count of the best top- k k retrieved chunks. We then select the long-context condition whose haystack character count most closely matches that retrieval character count. For example, the best top- k k retrieved context for the 1M-character haystack contains 217,152 characters; we therefore compare this retrieval condition against the 200K-character long-context condition, since the two inputs match most closely in character budget. Throughout, “context length” denotes character count rather than token count. sections.heading: Observations.
sections.text: Figure 12 shows that the relative advantage of top- k k ranked retrieval versus randomly sampled long-context prompting depends strongly on the model. Since each cell reports Δ = Ans RAG − Ans LC \Delta=\mathrm{Ans}_{\mathrm{RAG}}-\mathrm{Ans}_{\mathrm{LC}} , positive values indicate that the top- k k retrieved context performs better, whereas negative values indicate that the randomly sampled long-context haystack performs better. Overall, top- k k ranked retrieval competes strongly with long-context prompting under the matched character-budget setting. For GPT-4o, retrieval outperforms long-context prompting in four of the five matched budgets: 50K ( + 31 +31 pp), 70K ( + 22 +22 pp), 100K ( + 28 +28 pp), and 200K ( + 9 +9 pp). GPT-4o therefore benefits substantially when we replace the larger randomly sampled haystack with a compact retrieval-ranked context. GPT-5 also shows near parity between the two settings, with deltas close to zero across all budgets ( + 3 +3 , 0 0 , + 3 +3 , + 6 +6 , and 0 0 pp). For GPT-5, once the retrieved top- k k context contains the relevant evidence, the additional surrounding haystack context provides little or no answer-accuracy benefit. In contrast, GPT-4.1 consistently favors the randomly sampled long-context haystack. Its deltas remain negative at every matched budget, ranging from − 9 -9 pp at 100K to − 34 -34 pp at 90K. GPT-4.1 therefore exploits information from the broader haystack context more effectively than from the compact top- k k context, even when the retrieved context contains the necessary gold evidence. The Claude models show a similar but weaker long-context preference. Sonnet-4 improves under long-context prompting at 50K, 70K, 90K, and 100K, with the largest gain at 90K ( − 31 -31 pp), but retrieval performs slightly better at 200K ( + 6 +6 pp). Sonnet-4.5 also favors long-context prompting at most matched budgets, especially 90K ( − 25 -25 pp) and 100K ( − 16 -16 pp), while matching retrieval at 50K and showing only a small long-context advantage at 200K ( − 6 -6 pp). O3-mini swings unpredictably across budgets in both directions: long-context prompting helps at 50K ( − 12 -12 pp), retrieval helps at 70K and 200K ( + 12 +12 pp and + 9 +9 pp), and the two settings tie at 90K and 100K. A notable pattern emerges at the 90K budget, which favors long-context prompting most strongly. Four models show large negative deltas: GPT-4o ( − 25 -25 ,pp), GPT-4.1 ( − 34 -34 ,pp), Sonnet-4 ( − 31 -31 ,pp), and Sonnet-4.5 ( − 25 -25 ,pp). Evidence completeness therefore does not guarantee retrieval superiority. Even when the top- k k context contains the required needles, the model may benefit from broader discourse, surrounding distractors, or positional structure of the original haystack. Retrieval can therefore alter the contextual relationships through which evidence is interpreted, making compression effectiveness model-dependent. Conversely, strong positive deltas for GPT-4o and near-zero deltas for GPT-5 show that compact retrieval removes distractor burden without hurting accuracy for some models. Overall, the results do not support a single universal winner between randomly sampled haystacks and top- k k ranked retrieval. They instead reveal a model-specific tradeoff. Top- k k retrieval outperforms long-context prompting when compact evidence-focused contexts help the model avoid distraction, as GPT-4o demonstrates most clearly. Long-context prompting outperforms retrieval when models benefit from the broader haystack context, as GPT-4.1 and the Claude models demonstrate. GPT-5 emerges as the most retrieval-robust model in this comparison, showing that a sufficiently strong model answers equally well from the compact retrieved context and the matched randomly sampled haystack.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We compare Embedding-RAG and Reranker-FixedTopk-RAG across four LLMs. For each LC-matched budget in Table 15 , Embedding-RAG retrieves full-coverage top- k k chunks by cosine similarity. Reranker-RAG uses the same chunks and preserves the top- k k and character budget, but re-orders them using Qwen3-Reranker-8B relevance scores. No chunks are added or removed; the pipelines differ only in evidence ordering. This comparison isolates whether placing relevant evidence earlier improves generation rather than conflating ranking quality with context volume. With evidence availability and context size fixed, differences can be attributed to ranking and reveal whether models benefit from prioritizing relevant chunks. We evaluate both pipelines with our EBG prompt over n = 8 n=8 examples, comprising four needles under one-hop and two-hop queries. Results appear in Table 16 .

sections.heading: Observations.
sections.text: Table 16 shows that reranking improves end-to-end answer accuracy over embedding-based retrieval, with gains particularly pronounced at larger context budgets. Sonnet-4.5 benefits consistently from reranking, reaching 100% accuracy from 50K–100K and retaining an advantage at 200K. GPT-OSS-120B exhibits the largest gain at longer contexts, improving from 62.5% to 100% at 100K and from 50% to 87.5% at 200K. GPT-4.1 and GLM-5.2 also improve in most settings, although reranking is not uniformly beneficial: GPT-4.1 drops from 87.5% to 75% at 100K, while GLM-5.2 drops from 62.5% to 50% at 50K and remains unchanged at 90K. Overall, across the 20 model–budget combinations, Reranker-RAG improves over Embedding-RAG in 15 cases, ties in three, and underperforms in only two, indicating that improved evidence ordering can translate into better downstream answer generation even when the retrieved context budget is fixed. The larger gains at higher budgets suggest that retrieval quality remains important even when more context is available, particularly as irrelevant passages increasingly compete for the reader’s attention. Because both pipelines contain identical chunks, these gains isolate ordering rather than evidence availability, suggesting that readers are sensitive to where relevant evidence appears within the retrieved context. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY-SA 4.0 arXiv:2610.26951v1 [cs.CL] 18 Oct 2026 The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering Debopriyo Banerjee Owais Aijaz Ahmer Tabassum Zhuohan Xie Affiliation: MBZUAI {deb.ban89, vesko.st}@gmail.com preslav.nakov@mbzuai.ac.ae Project Code Preslav Nakov Affiliation: MBZUAI {deb.ban89, vesko.st}@gmail.com preslav.nakov@mbzuai.ac.ae Project Code Veselin Stoyanov Affiliation: MBZUAI {deb.ban89, vesko.st}@gmail.com preslav.nakov@mbzuai.ac.ae Project Code Affiliation: Inception42 Abstract Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the dominant paradigm for grounding large language models in external corpora, but its similarity-driven, chunked pipeline has structural blind spots: it cannot anticipate which passages a question requires and discards document-level context that resolves cross-passage references. We introduce evidence-based generation (EBG), requiring models to return an answer with line-level citations, and a joint Ans+Evid metric that scores correctness and grounding simultaneously. We reformulate two corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document QA benchmarks - MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP , a multi-paper adaptation of QASPER with realistic short paper cues, and pair them with a controlled synthetic two-hop haystack and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K–1M characters. Across ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs, EBG isolates two RAG limitations that long-context models avoid: similarity retrieval surfaces any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi-fact queries, and chunking destroys document meta-information needed to resolve identity-bearing queries. EBG also exposes grounding failures invisible to answer-only evaluation, including incomplete citations in two-needle settings and a widening gap between Ans and Ans+Evid when context contradicts parametric knowledge. Data and code are available at https://github.com/debobanerjee/LC-EBG . 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) can rapidly process large text volumes to identify information relevant to a query. This capability suits applications such as legal discovery, medical analysis, financial due diligence, literature review, etc., which require synthesis from large document collections. The predominant paradigm for grounding LLM outputs in external knowledge is retrieval-augmented generation ( Lewis et al., 2020 , RAG;) , which retrieves passages via embedding similarity and conditions the generator on those passages alone. While effective for single-fact lookups , this design has several structural limitations. First, each retrieved chunk is stripped of its surrounding context: the model cannot see where a paragraph falls within a document or how it relates to neighboring sections. Second, document-level metadata (authorship, date, section hierarchy) is typically lost during chunking. Third, and most critically, similarity-based retrieval cannot anticipate which combination of passages will be needed for questions requiring integration across multiple locations. This is particularly acute for multi-hop questions , where the answer depends on chaining facts that may appear in distant, semantically dissimilar passages ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Our goal in this paper is not to advocate replacing RAG with long-context (LC) models outright, but to make these structural limitations measurable. RAG systems are typically evaluated on answer correctness alone, which conflates two very different failure modes: the retriever fails to surface the right passages, or the reader fails to use them. To separate the two, we propose evidence-based generation (EBG) , a paradigm where the model must produce both an answer and explicit references to the input lines that support it. EBG inherits RAG’s built-in verifiability ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) , but extends it to long-context settings where the model is given the full document neighborhood and must select its own evidence. The joint Ans+Evid metric pinpoints where a pipeline breaks: in retrieval, in grounding, or in reading. Recent work shows LC models can match or exceed RAG accuracy given sufficient context ( Li et al., 2024 ; Laitenberger et al., 2025 ) , but without provenance these comparisons are inconclusive; EBG closes that gap. We make the following contributions: • EBG framework. We define the evidence-based generation task and a joint Ans+Evid metric, and evaluate ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs under matched LC and RAG conditions across 10K–1M character contexts. • Evidence-grounded benchmarks. We reformulate two corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document QA benchmarks—a re-instrumented MultiHop-RAG with line-level evidence labels, and QASPER-MP , a multi-paper QASPER adaptation with realistic paper cues, and pair them with a controlled two-hop synthetic haystack and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa . The first two stress retrieval; the last two stress long-context reading. • Characterizing RAG’s limitations. Using EBG, we isolate two failure modes of similarity-based RAG that LC sidesteps: (i) retrieval recovers any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi-fact queries, and (ii) chunking discards document meta-information that identity-bearing queries depend on. On MultiHop-RAG , the retrieval ceiling at realistic top-k budgets, not the reader, is the binding constraint. • Diagnostic analysis of LC grounding. Beyond the RAG comparison, EBG reveals that citation acts as a reasoning scaffold, that models cite incomplete evidence in two-needle settings, and that grounding degrades sharply when in-context evidence contradicts parametric knowledge. 2 Related Work 2.1 Long-Context Language Models Advances in transformer architectures have expanded context windows from thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens through improved positional encoding such as ALiBi ( Press et al., 2022 ) , RoPE extensions ( Su et al., 2024 ) , and memory-augmented attention ( Wu et al., 2022 ) . Training data matters equally, as pretraining corpora rarely contain long-range dependencies; Zhuang et al. (2025) construct data with long-distance references encouraging use of distant context. Yet larger windows do not automatically yield better reasoning. Du et al. (2025) show accuracy degrades with context length even under perfect retrieval, suggesting a processing bottleneck. Similarly, Liu et al. (2024) show performance drops when information appears mid-input rather than at boundaries. 2.2 Evaluating Long-Context Reasoning Early long-context evaluations relied on needle-in-a-haystack tests ( Kamradt, 2024 ) , which mainly measure retrieval of planted information rather than reasoning. Subsequent work argues that such evaluations set the bar too low, since strong performance often reflects shallow heuristics rather than genuine understanding ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Schuster et al., 2025 ; Modarressi et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Yen et al., 2025 ) . Recent benchmarks shift toward more demanding evaluations: ∞ \infty Bench ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) studies degradation beyond 100K characters, HELMET ( Yen et al., 2025 ) shows that benchmark choice substantially alters rankings, and NoLiMa ( Modarressi et al., 2025 ) removes lexical shortcuts by requiring semantic matching between queries and evidence. However, these benchmarks still score models on final answers alone, leaving open whether correct answers stem from actual use of relevant context or from priors, surface cues, or chance. Unlike these answer-only benchmarks, our work focuses on grounding by requiring models to return both answers and supporting input lines, distinguishing genuine reasoning from lucky guessing and enabling a more faithful assessment of whether models use long contexts effectively and reliably. 2.3 Retrieval-Augmented Generation Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) remains the dominant approach for grounding LLMs in external knowledge. Built on dense retrieval ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ) and multi-passage readers such as Fusion-in-Decoder ( Izacard and Grave, 2021 ) , RAG provides provenance by construction since retrieved passages serve as evidence. Recent work revisits RAG alongside long-context models, highlighting a trade-off between the two paradigms ( Li et al., 2024 ; Laitenberger et al., 2025 ) : long-context prompting generally improves accuracy but at substantially higher cost, motivating hybrid systems that route queries by difficulty ( Li et al., 2024 ) . Controlled comparisons also show well-tuned single-stage RAG can match elaborate multi-stage pipelines once token budgets are equalized ( Laitenberger et al., 2025 ) , while adaptive retrieval and self-reflection improve factuality and citation quality ( Asai et al., 2024 ) . Existing work primarily evaluates these approaches on accuracy or efficiency. We instead focus on grounding, distinguishing whether evidence was available from whether the model actually used it. 3 Evidence-based Generation (EBG) We formalize evidence-based generation (EBG) as a grounded question-answering paradigm that extends standard answer-only evaluation by requiring models to generate both answers and explicit citations to the supporting input evidence. 3.1 Answer-only vs Evidence-based Generation Existing long-context evaluations, including NoLiMa ( Modarressi et al., 2025 ) , use answer-only evaluation, omitting the grounding needed to validate model reasoning. EBG extends this formulation by requiring models to generate both explicit evidence references to supporting input lines and the final answer , yielding a stricter evaluation setting in which correctness depends on both accurate reasoning and faithful grounding. To illustrate the distinction, consider a haystack containing the sentence “Then Stuart mentioned that he has been vegan for years.” at line 1,284 and the question “Which character cannot eat Brandade?” - a two-hop query requiring the inference that Brandade contains fish and is therefore incompatible with veganism . The answer-only and EBG settings differ in both the system instruction and the required output format. Answer-only Prompt (User) You will answer a question based on the following book snippet: {haystack} Use the information provided in the book snippet to answer the question. Your answer should be short and based on either explicitly stated facts or strong, logical inferences. Question: Which character cannot eat Brandade? Return only the final answer with no additional explanation or reasoning. Model Response Stuart Under answer-only evaluation, the response ‘‘Stuart’’ is simply marked correct. But under EBG, the same response is evaluated using three complementary metrics: answer accuracy ( Ans ), evidence accuracy ( Evid ), and their conjunction ( Ans+Evid ). While Ans preserves standard answer correctness, Ans+Evid additionally requires the model to cite the supporting evidence at line 1,284. Together, these metrics separate answer correctness from evidence-grounded correctness. EBG Prompt (System + User) [system] Your job is to answer the question entirely from the context and provide a reference. Your answer should cite all lines the answer is based on. [user] <context>{haystack}</context> Answer the question based on information only from the context. If the question is not answerable from the context, answer NA. Your response should comprise only the answer and all lines the answer is based on in json format. For example: { ‘‘lines’’: [25, 412],‘‘answer’’: ‘‘John’’ } Question: Which character cannot eat Brandade? Model Response { ‘‘lines’’: [1284], ‘‘answer’’: ‘‘Stuart’’ } This decomposition exposes silent failures hidden by answer-only evaluation: a model may arrive at the correct answer while citing irrelevant lines, or retrieve the correct evidence while producing the wrong answer. The joint Ans+Evid metric therefore serves as the strictest measure of evidence-based reasoning, requiring both accurate reasoning and faithful grounding. We also evaluate vanilla Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, following Modarressi et al. (2025) , and a CoT-based EBG prompting variant. The prompt templates are in Appendix A . 3.2 RAG under EBG In this work, we evaluate RAG systems within the EBG framework by requiring models to not only answer using retrieved chunks, but also to explicitly cite the supporting evidence. This yields two RAG variants: • Answer-only RAG: Standard formulation requiring answer correctness only. • Answer + Evidence RAG: EBG formulation requiring correct answer and correct citation. This unified view allows us to decompose end-to-end performance into two factors: • Evidence availability: whether the retriever surfaces the relevant needle(s) (Hit@k), • Evidence utilization: whether the model correctly uses and cites the retrieved evidence (long-context accuracy). Overall, our formulation shows that RAG and EBG are not competing paradigms but complementary components : retrieval determines what evidence is available , while EBG determines whether that evidence is correctly used and cited . 4 Benchmarks To systematically evaluate EBG and RAG under EBG, we construct four complementary benchmarks: a fully synthetic benchmark, an evidence-augmented version of NoLiMa, MultiHop-RAG, and QASPER-MP (an adapted version of QASPER). Together, they evaluate EBG under both controlled synthetic settings and realistic long-context scenarios. 4.1 Synthetic Dataset The synthetic benchmark provides precise control over haystack content and evidence placement. It consists of a distractor fact pool, a curated needle set, and a haystack generation procedure. This controlled construction allows us to vary context length independently of task difficulty while retaining exact ground-truth evidence locations. Distractor fact pool. We construct a fixed pool of 66,834 unique single-sentence facts using iterative LLM prompting followed by deduplication, ensuring that distractors are not confusable with inserted needles. The large pool also limits repeated distractors across independently generated trials and provides sufficient diversity for constructing long haystacks. Needle set. We manually curate 10 two-hop needles , each containing: i) two atomic supporting facts, ii) a compositional question requiring both facts, and iii) accepted answer surface forms. The needles span relations such as company–product associations, founder–specialty links, and birthplace lookups. By requiring composition across two independently placed facts, the benchmark tests both evidence retrieval and integration rather than simple single-fact recall. Haystack assembly. For a target length L L , distractor facts are shuffled and accumulated until reaching L L characters, after which the two needle facts are inserted at independently sampled positions and recorded as gold evidence. Haystacks are formatted as line-numbered i: fact entries and evaluated under the EBG prompt template (§ A ). Each trial uses a newly generated haystack and a uniformly sampled needle. Consequently, performance differences cannot be attributed to a fixed ordering of distractors or evidence positions. Appendix B.1 provides a representative example. Sanity check. At L = 10 ​ K L{=}10\text{K} ( ≈ 2 ​ K {\approx}2\text{K} tokens), all evaluated frontier models achieve at least 0.98 0.98 joint Ans+Evid accuracy over N = 100 N{=}100 trials, confirming that the inserted needles are unambiguous and readily solvable when context length is modest. Any degradation at larger L L therefore reflects failures in long-context evidence retrieval or integration rather than intrinsic task ambiguity. This makes the synthetic benchmark a controlled probe of how model reliability changes as relevant evidence becomes increasingly sparse within the surrounding context. 4.2 NoLiMa-based Dataset We adapt the NoLiMa haystack construction procedure to create long-context inputs ranging from L = 10 ​ K L{=}10\text{K} to 1 ​ M 1\text{M} characters and require models to both answer questions and cite supporting needles as evidence. This converts NoLiMa from an answer-only benchmark into an evidence-grounded evaluation that tests whether models truly use the provided context. Needle set. We use the original single-needle (SN) setting from NoLiMa ( Modarressi et al., 2025 ) , specifically the 0402 and 0405 needle groups with both default and inverse variants under the commonsense category. Each needle contains a character name and a single factual attribute, and supports both one-hop and two-hop questions. We further introduce a two-needle ( TN ) setting, in which the explicit secondary needle is consistent with world knowledge, and a contradictory two-needle ( CTN ) variant, in which it conflicts with world knowledge. Appendix C.1 provides additional details and templates for SN , TN , and CTN settings. Haystack assembly. We adopt the random book generation procedure from NoLiMa ( Modarressi et al., 2025 ) to construct haystacks ranging from 10K to 1M characters (10K–50K in 10K increments and 100K–1M in 100K increments), generating three random books B 1 c , B 2 c , B 3 c {B^{c}_{1},B^{c}_{2},B^{c}_{3}} for each context length c c . Because tokenization is model-dependent, we vary input length in characters rather than tokens. Each haystack is split into line-indexed entries using the ‘\n’ delimiter. In the single-needle setting, the needle is inserted at one of four normalized depths: 0, 0.33, 0.67, or 1.0. In the two-needle setting, the primary needle is fixed at depth 0.5, while the secondary needle is inserted at one of the same four depths. 4.3 Multi-document QA Datasets To stress the retrieval pipeline on the dimensions it is meant to handle, we reformulate two existing corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document question answering (QA) benchmarks. Both are designed to make RAG’s retrieval-vs.-reading split observable: gold evidence is labeled at the line (sentence or paragraph) level, so the same scoring code works for LC and any retriever-ordered context. MultiHop-RAG ( Tang and Yang, 2024 ) . The official release contains 609 news articles (4.6M characters, 1.2M tokens with the cl100k_base tokenizer) and 2,556 queries in four templated types: inference , comparison , temporal , and null_query (unanswerable). Each non-null query carries an evidence_list of 2–4 gold facts , each consisting of a source article title and an exact textual span. Removing the 301 null_query items leaves 2,255 usable queries ; for the pilot reported in this paper, we uniformly sample 50 queries (seed 0), naturally stratified across the three answerable types ( n inf = 13 n_{\text{inf}}{=}13 , n comp = 21 n_{\text{comp}}{=}21 , n temp = 16 n_{\text{temp}}{=}16 ). For the LC condition, we construct an oracle-containing per-query mini-haystack comprising every gold-evidence article plus 20 distractor articles sampled from the remainder of the corpus. The articles are concatenated in random order and split into sentence-per-line entries, producing contexts of approximately 241K characters on average. For the RAG condition, we perform open-corpus retrieval over the full 609-article corpus: we divide the corpus into 256-token sliding windows (6,296 chunks), embed the chunks with text-embedding-3-large , and rank them by cosine similarity to produce top- K K contexts for K ∈ { 4 , 10 , 25 , 50 , 100 , 200 } K\in\{4,10,25,50,100,200\} . The two conditions are therefore not pool-matched: LC evaluates reading and evidence utilization when all gold source articles are guaranteed present, whereas RAG must first retrieve the required evidence from the full corpus. Accordingly, this experiment diagnoses the contribution of open-corpus retrieval failures to end-to-end performance; it is not a direct LC–RAG comparison under identical candidate pools. In both conditions, gold facts are re-mapped to line numbers inside the assembled context; in RAG, a gold fact that is not retrieved has no corresponding gold line. Appendix D reports the corresponding retrieval ceilings (Hits@ k k for any vs. all gold facts) and reproduces the answer-only RAG baselines from the original paper. QASPER-MP . QASPER ( Dasigi et al., 2021 ) contains 5,049 information-seeking questions over 1,585 NLP papers, each annotated by domain experts with paragraph-level evidence and a short free-form or extractive answer (including Unanswerable ). The original task is single-document and, therefore, does not exercise the retrieval pipeline. We construct QASPER-MP (multi-paper) by pairing each gold paper with ten distractor papers sampled from the QASPER pool, yielding an 11-paper haystack per query, and rewrite every question to include a realistic paper cue - in ∼ \sim 50% of cases a first-author surname (e.g., “Smith et al.”), and otherwise a 2–3 word verbatim title fragment - split by a hash of the question id. This forces the system to resolve document identity from a realistic cue rather than the full paper title. The task jointly tests document identification, evidence localization, and answer generation. Since distractors come from the same NLP-paper collection, they provide domain-matched context. A successful system must identify the relevant paper and supporting paragraph(s) before answering, while retaining QASPER’s expert-annotated answers and evidence. For LC, papers are serialized in an XML-like format that preserves titles, abstracts, and section structure ( <paper> , <title> , <abstract> , <section> ); paragraphs are line-numbered, and the same paragraph-level gold labels are used for evidence scoring. For RAG, we evaluate both a flat variant (concatenate the top- K K retrieved paragraphs in rank order) and a structured variant that re-emits the surrounding <paper> / <title> / <abstract> scaffolding and inserts “ ... ” markers for discontinuities, so that retrieved fragments retain their document provenance. We evaluate QASPER-MP at two scales. For proprietary models, we conduct a pilot on N = 50 N{=}50 queries, comprising 38 answerable and 12 unanswerable examples. For open-weight models, we expand the evaluation to N = 200 N{=}200 queries, providing broader benchmark coverage and a more stable estimate of aggregate performance. Because the proprietary-model results are based on the smaller pilot, comparisons across the two model groups should be interpreted with the corresponding difference in sampling uncertainty in mind. RQ1: LC-EBG addresses two RAG limitations. On MultiHop-RAG , queries require 2–4 evidence facts spread across distinct articles, so faithful answering requires the retriever to surface all required facts within its top- k k budget. For this benchmark, the two conditions use different evidence-access regimes: open-corpus RAG searches 6,296 chunks constructed from all 609 articles , whereas the oracle-containing LC condition receives every gold-evidence article plus 20 distractor articles. The conditions are therefore not pool-matched; this comparison diagnoses the cost of open-corpus retrieval relative to reading when the gold source articles are guaranteed to be available. We first reproduce the answer-only RAG baselines from the original benchmark under our pipeline ( text-embedding-3-large + 256-token windows; Appendix D ) and measure annotated-gold retrieval coverage directly. At k = 10 k{=}10 , the retriever covers any gold fact for 82 % 82\% of queries but covers all gold facts for only 19 % 19\% (and just 8 % 8\% on inference queries). When the gold annotations are exhaustive and every annotated fact is necessary, all-gold coverage bounds the faithfully grounded performance of the downstream RAG reader. Under answer-only prompting, open-corpus RAG at k = 200 k{=}200 reaches parity with the oracle-containing LC condition only for Sonnet-4.5 ( 68 % 68\% vs. 68 % 68\% ). See Appendix F.4 for more details. 6 Conclusion and Future Work We introduced evidence-based generation (EBG) , a framework that requires models to produce both an answer and line-level citations, together with a joint Ans+Evid metric that measures correctness and grounding simultaneously. By separating retrieval from evidence-grounded reasoning, EBG exposes failures obscured by answer-only evaluation. We evaluate these failures using evidence-grounded versions of MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP , a controlled synthetic two-hop haystack, and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K–1M characters. This evaluation suite spans both realistic and controlled settings, allowing retrieval, reasoning, and grounding errors to be examined under complementary conditions. Across ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs, EBG reveals two key RAG limitations: (i) similarity retrieval finds any relevant chunk more reliably than all evidence required for multi-fact queries, imposing a retrieval ceiling at realistic top- k k budgets; and (ii) chunking can discard document-level meta-information needed by identity-bearing queries, causing RAG to over-refuse on retrieval misses. EBG further exposes grounding failures hidden by answer-only metrics: models often cite incomplete evidence, and the gap between answer and joint accuracy widens when in-context evidence conflicts with parametric knowledge. These findings show that correct answers alone can substantially overstate a model’s ability to faithfully use long-context evidence. They also highlight evidence attribution as a useful diagnostic for distinguishing retrieval limitations from downstream reasoning failures. Consequently, EBG provides a more informative basis for comparing RAG and long-context systems than evaluations that collapse retrieval, reasoning, and attribution into answer accuracy alone.
